title: Brand-new subscriber after abandoning Sci Am - great so far!
text:
After years of growing disgust with Scientific American (I've been a subscriber to Sci Am since 1975), I vented my frustration with SciAm by writing a scathing review on Amazon tonight. After writing the review, I perused the numerous other reviews from frustrated former SciAm lovers. Several of them recommended AmSci. I spent an hour checking out the AmSci website and I was hooked. I gave them my credit card and I am now a proud subscriber! Long live AmSci, good riddance to SciAm.

Will update this review as often as needed. The only reason I gave it 4 out of 5 stars is because AmSci has only 6 issues a year - not enough! Make it a monthly and I will raise my rating to 5 stars!

[Update Feb 27, 2011]
Now that my first print copy has arrived, I am glad to report that I am very, very pleased. Sci Am could learn a lot by looking at Am Sci. The magazine is dense! There is hardly any whitespace. Photos and illustrations are not full-page, but they add essential information. The articles are satisfying, thought-provoking and rigorous. Each one is written by a real, working scientist or full professor. I actually LEARNED things from this issue, instead of (as in the case of Sci Am), fuming about errors. And the book reviews! What a delight - about 6 pages of reviews! Each review was thorough, detailed, and nearly a page long.

Instead of stupid politics, there was a great essay on ethics in science.

I still wish this was a monthly! I would gladly pay twice as much for 12 issues a year.

The contrast between AmSci and SciAm is extreme. My March issue of SciAm went largely unread; I have put it on the shelf without finishing it. When my current SciAm subscription lapses, I will not renew. Instead, I plan to donate what I would have spend on SciAm to AmSci!

title: The sad, sad demise of a once-great magazine...
text:
UPDATE - an hour after I wrote the following review I checked out American Scientist magazine - I am now a proud subscriber. AmSci is everything that SciAm used to be! I'll keep my SciAm subscription for another year, and then will probably drop SciAm.

I'm so frustrated with Sci Am I could scream. I've been a subscriber since 1975; I have all the back issues lovingly stored in expensive magazine cases. I used to look forward to each new issue with excited, joyful anticipation. Now I dread the arrival of each pitiful rag. The only reason I have not dropped my subscription is the fading hope that they will fire most of the editorial board, starting with DiChristina, who is doing her best to morph SciAm into a Frankenstein's Monster of Popular Science (she used to be the editor of PopSci).

The "new" format is just another step down the long road to failure. The glued-binding keeps the magazine from sitting flat on a table, and if a page is torn there is no easy way to repair it.

It is distressingly skinny, a mere 82-96 pages per issue. When I complain about this, the response is that paper and ink are so, so terribly expensive - but if that is the problem, why do they squander page after page with either full-color pictures and graphics that add nothing to the content, or even worse, waste almost all of a page with nothing at all - no text, no images? Can't they afford to pay for a few thousand more words to fill the empty space? Here's a list of the wasted pages in the January 2011 issue: 34,35,40,41,46,47,half of 52, 53,58,65,half of 69,72,78, half of 79 and half of 88! This represents nearly 20% of the pages available for non-advertising content!

The layout has moved some of the few remaining decent features such as "50,100 & 150 Years Ago" to the back of the magazine. Even worse, the middle now has "feature articles" that are only two or three pages and a few hundred words long (because they are mostly whitespace or useless photos).

In the current issue, only two "full length" articles are written by actual research scientists - the rest of the fluff is penned by "science writers" from failing institutions such as the New York Times or grad students! Issue after issue goes by without a single equation appearing anywhere (except in ads for software)

Even the few decent articles, written by real scientists have been shortened to 6 pages or less, and the quality of the writing has deteriorated. Even as recently as 2004 I would LEARN things when I read Sci Am; now I am teased, confused and forced to research on the web to figure out what the author was trying to express, or (even worse) spending time scribbling corrections in the margins.

Long gone are former delights such as "Mathematical Games" or the "Amateur Scientist"

The content is consistently, disturbingly political, and always slanted to the left. I'm no right-winger, but anyone with a shred of objectivity can see the blatant bias that permeates the magazine. Essay after essay bemoaning human-caused climate change by hacks that can't do simple math that would tell them that if every one of the fruitless carbon-saving recommendations were adopted, the reduction in greenhouse gases would amount to an insignificant fraction of the total atmospheric mass of same. Every point in the "Political Wish List" on page 12 is stupid and just plain incorrect - ignoring for the moment the idiocy of even having a page devoted to a "Political Wish List" in a magazine purportedly devoted to science!

Even in the esoteric realm of theoretical physics, you will no longer find any essay that does not toe the "superstrings or the highway" mindset.

I'm not sure if circulation has increased since the dumbing-down started, and I really don't care. If it has gone up, it just means that I have nothing in common with the new subscriber base.

I'm genuinely freaked-out and at a loss. I don't want to see a gap in my unbroken swath of issues, but it galls me every time I write a check and send it to this bunch of losers. Perhaps I should just go to Walmart and snap hi-res photos of every page of every new issue, print and bind them, and wait until I see the problems have been corrected before sending them any more of my hard-earned money!

Disgusted,

Steve Crye

title: Worthless for refrigerator reviews
text: I bought the $35 digital subscription directly from the Consumer Reports site in order to get their reviews on refrigerators.  After sifting through tons of reviews, I found an inverse relationship between CR's ratings and user reviews:  high CR ratings for reliability and user satisfaction correlate with large numbers of user complaints and dissatisfaction.  In one case, CR flagged a GE frig as having low user satisfaction, but the user reviews on the CR site are ALL positive with NO complaints.  CR used to be a good place to get guidance on products, but evidently not any more, and I can't imagine what they're basing their ratings on.  In any case, I've concluded Consumer Reports is a waste of time and money.

When my daughter was diagnosed with Celiac I started to read everything I could about Gluten free. I also want to mention that their customer service was exceptional. When my magazine failed to start on time I sent them an email and within a day I had a response, a magazine in the mail and a personal follow-up a week later to ensure I got it.
All of these things very much impress me about this magazine.
I know sometimes people write great reviews and they turn out to be affiliated with the company. I am just a mom with an adult child that went through a lot over the past 2 years, and this magazine has really been a joy for both of us. If you are going to pick just one Gluten Free periodical, this would be the one.

title: Ms., this is not!
text:
I'm not going to say that Bust isn't a decent magazine. And if other feminist publications weren't around, I'd probably be reading it cover to cover. The problem is that they seem to assume that everyone who reads their mag is all do-it-yourself-y and artsy. And that they're actually interested in clothing. I'm not. I still appreciate some of the articles -- for example, the article several months ago on the womanly diagnosis of "hysteria" and this latest issue's article about American women converting to Islam.

If you're a knitter, cool. If you're a sorta-kinda feminist, cool. If you just want to read something that isn't telling you to go out and find a husband, like, yesterday, this is a good mag too. But if you're looking for something that is a little more FEMINIST, pick up Bitch magazine.

title: Every woman (and man) needs to read this magazine!
text:
Ms. magazine has been one of my favorites for years. Its not very easy to find. but many libraries have a subscription to it. As you can see, its quite expensive for a yearly subscription, but it is well worth it!
Ms. is a magazine written from a feminist point of view. People like Gloria Steinhem are frequent contributors. There is no random male-bashing that goes on between these covers, however; everything written is well thought out and backed up with factual information. Along with articles about various womens' issues, sexism in the United States, etc., there is usually an article in each issue about what is going on for women and other minority groups in the rest of the world, especially third-world countries.
This magazine is a definite great buy for anyone who has an interest in womens' rights; stories are often written from a fresh point-of-view you can't find anywhere else. I also like to curl up with one of my old issues whenever I need to get MAD about something; there is always a special focus on the underdog and her plight.

title: Essential for the Individual Investor
text:
You need to read IBD if you invest in stocks. It's a unique and must-read newspaper for an individual investor. It is filled with solid information about stock and company characteristics. It focuses on market areas targeted to small investors. It's totally different from WSJ, broker resources and other investment news options. IBD is designed around a specific investment method, so once you understand the method the information is particularly easy to assimilate. The usefulness of the information is adaptable to many investment styles, such as those implementing Jim Cramer's rules. Just a few of its daily columns are worth the price of a subscription.

What about the op-ed views? If you're a libertarian or libertarian-conservative, you'll appreciate IBD's perspective. You won't agree all the time, but it's op-eds are well-informed and thought provoking. You can ignore the op-eds if you're uncomfortable with liberty and prefer a more statist approach.

title: A Superb, Thoughtful Monthly Magazine!
text:
In the several years since my retirement, I have come to wait by my trusty old rusted metal mailbox around the third or fourth of every month, waiting for my monthly issue of two magazines, the Atlantic Monthly and Harpers. Each in iuts own way is likely the best amalgams of intellectual articles on a variety of subjects one can find in contemporary America, and each features a stable of highly regarded writers and authors. For good reason; from subjects as arcane as the supposed imminent fall of the Soviet union based on demographic and economic analysis in the mid-1980s to the recent synopsis of former spy Robert Baer regarding the evils of dealing with the highly corrupted Saudi regime, the magazine consistently offers an erudite, informative, and provocative look at aspects of contemporary reality one cannot find elsewhere.

Needless to say, I really enjoy reading Harpers, especially under the guidance of editor Lewis lapham, and its articles often lead me on Amazon searches for tomes by the talented authors, which in the case of said author Robert Baer, or perpetually sagacious satirist P.J. O'Rourke, or a whole raft of noteable others. All of them lead to some worthwhile reading experiences indeed. It avoids the trendy, so we are spared the suffering through the latest and greatest mass experiences in favor of intellectual roads less traveled, being grassy and rather wont of wear, makes for better and more satisfying traveling, whether trudging through the snow with my Wintertime Dunham Tyroleans or padding down grassy fields in my summertime Birkenstocks. Just keep on trucking! Enjoy!

title: The gift of human speech.
text:
I think a very few magazines can boast of getting better and better with the years.
GQ is one of these exceptions. While most of the competitors insult you by presuming your attention span does not exceed 5-6 minutes the magazine presents you with the articles that are sometimes 6-7 pages long and very profound. It took Robert Draper 2 month to research the eunuch subculture in the modern USA (April 2000) but the resulting piece of journalism is unforgettable - just as the guy's feature on the once-famous bodybuilder, the reluctant muscle god Dave Draper. I still smile recalling some of Joe Queenan's Parisian pranks - the Froggies finally got their due. And the author puts something really funny in almost every issue.
The sophisticated grumpiness of Alan Richman makes his every visit to a restaurant at home and abroad a real clash of the concepts how things should be and how they really are - these modes rarely meet in space and time but when it happens the gourmet is the first to heap the praise. And there are also The Style Guy, the monthly advice how to get rid of these annoying extra twenty grand - with a taste and style, Adam Sach's musings on the things that come his way and a lot more.
Yeah, you get your hundreds pages of the latest fashion which is also a reason to buy the GQ but the glossiness can be found in many other places. The magazine talks to you in the voices of people you'd surely like to have as friends. There is no elitism, no showing off, no "entertaining" silliness. The authors' irony is endearing and mostly aimed at themselves. But do not get the impression it's small-scale. The magazine is very well-connected and you are guaranteed to get the interviews with and the profiles of all the celebrities you'd like to hear about. The persons which interest me no less are these common people you'll have no chance to meet reading the rest of the "men's magazines". The need to sell many sorts of fashionable merchandise and to form the yearning for a lot of expensive non-essential stuff is coped with somehow - the magazine had not lost the most precious gift - the gift of human speech.

title: Be careful of their add-on offers
text:
I just renewed my online subscription to Consumers Report. When it was confirmed, I received a pop-up stating I could add the printed subscription for $15 more per year. When the pop-up appeared, it blacked out the rest of the screen so I couldn't see the SAME offer in the corner for $12.

I thought, oh well, they got me. No big deal. They got me for $3, not worth the effort to complain for $3.

Then when I signed in to my online subscription, I received another ad stating I could purchase the same 12 month subscription for $14. Wow!! Isn't this the type of thing my Consumer's Reports is supposed to advise me about and help prevent me from being cheated?

There is a saying, 'Screw me once, shame on you. Screw me twice, shame on me.' Next year I won't renew. I won't give them the chance to screw me again. I thought this was the type of deceptive advertising Consumer's Reports was supposed to help prevent???

text:
Love this magazine beyond words. I've subscribed to it for about 20 years, and am still always thrilled when the newest issue comes in the mail. I love history, I love imagining how people lived in so many different cultures throughout the millenia. I love the investigation, the mystery, of discovering archaeological evidence and attempting to interpret and extrapolate. (I'm not an archeologist myself, so I live vicariously through the discoveries of others.) If you love social history, cultural psychology, or, of course, archaeology, you must must must subscribe to this magazine!

I subscribe to about 9 magazines that cover a broad range of topics. To avoid clutter, I read each issue soon after it arrives, tear out any particularly interesting articles, then recycle the magazine. However.... Archaeology is so beautiful, I so love revisiting the articles, that this is the one magazine for which I've saved every single issue. About 120 of them so far. I often pull out an old issue at random and reread it just for the fun of it. And with my middling memory, I always find something that I've forgotten. Wonderful!

I’m sorry, but I guess the magazines like this are pretty much past their usefulness. For me, that could backpacking magazine should have articles about backpacking with accompanied gear reviews that help me make informed decisions. For me, the articles are just OK, a bit like hiking through the high desert. It’s not terrible but at the same time there’s not very much to look at. What’s worse, is that the gear reviews are fairly dismal. They usually have very limited comparisons and stick to the more expensive brands (like oh, I don’t know, the ones that advertise in the magazine?). You can find much better reviews on reputable backpacking web sites.

I think that what killed it for me is the regional nature of the magazine now. A real backpacker wants to get away from where they live and experience other places. In their attempt to deliver targeted content they failed to engage me with articles about things that I don’t know about. For that, I’ll just stick to the discussion boards.

title: Love the Magazine, Love Rachael, It's the subscription offers that the problem
text:
As the title states, I love the magazine, and I love Rachael Ray - she's just great!

My problem is with the publishers and all the confusing information.
1. One year equals 12 months!
Wrong! One year is, ah ? 10 months!
When the magazine first came out, the offer was 1 FREE issue (11 issues total) for the rate of $18.00 - (The quoted Cover Price - $39.90 for 10 issues - what a DEAL!)

I received my "Summary of Account", and that Summary statement shows the cover price of $43.89 - WOW, my savings just went from 55% to 58%!

Today, I received my December/January 2007 Issue, and another renewal offer. They're offering me a great deal to renew about 10 months early! For 2 years (not 24 months of issues) for 20 issues, I get to pay them $29.98. Another 24 months puts me into 2009, or there abouts - My current subscription ends in October 2007.

Also today, in the mail, I received a separate offer (different return box number). I can give a "one year (10 issues)" gift subscription at an "adjusted rate" for $18.00.

Okay, so, should I give myself a gift for additional 10 issues at $18.00, or sign up for 20 issues for $29.98?? - I'm confused. The $29.98 deal sounds pretty good.

NOT! - Neither Offer. The idea that I'm going to renew and pay, (in other words, let them be my bank) my subscription about 1 year in advance is not gonna happen. I quit Reader's Digest, and maybe I'll be quitting Consumer's Report because they were/are always telling me I need to renew when I don't.

At least these offers aren't telling me my subscription is about to expire, - yet.

Guess this sort of marketing works or else they wouldn't do it. I just wish we'd be given their best offer and be done with it - crazy marketing. Just makes me wonder - really - how low can they go to get me back after I quit renewing because of all their antics.

Oh, LOVE THE MAGAZINE!

I wish they could print the magazine in "large" print or in a way that allows people like me who aren't really reading impaired, but left behind by Wired's weird print style. So, I do go online to read the digital version, but I love taking my favorite magazines with me to pull out when I am waiting for something or someone.  I keep several handy in my bag so I am never bored and eventually get the whole thing devoured over the month. It's very hard to hang on to Wired that long because before I can get it read, I have another edition that I need to tackle.  Friends have agreed that it is too much trouble to read it. title: The quintessential automotive magazine. What can I say?
text:
I subscribed to Hemmings at the urging of my neighbor who has a 1936 Ford.

I'm not a "car guy", but I do own and drive a really old car. It's not a hobby, it's just a dang nice (fun) car to drive and is very practical. Hemmings is really geared toward the car enthusiast, but even a non-car guy like me can find plenty of interesting stuff in here. It's about the size of a phone book, and feels rather hefty. Just full of stuff!

Some of the articles are written from the perspective that the reader will know what the writer is talking about when tossing around a lot of car-guy lingo. A lot of it goes over my head, so I skip some of the articles. Once in a while they write about something really good, and then I'm drawn in completely. I like cars of the brass era and early 30's, not at all in to muscle cars or especially not anything built after WW2, but this magazine has a good mix.

The "for sale" section takes up most of the magazine and that is where I spend the majority of the time. It's fun to look through all the stuff available, and I learn a lot from the ads in it too. Really interesting to see how many people sell parts and service for old cars. I admit to using some of the vendors because of their ads in Hemmings...

It's a little off-putting sometimes when things in the magazine are written with the assumption that every reader is a millionaire and they toss around values of "dream cars" like it's nothing. C'mon!!! How many Hemmings subscribers really have a 6-figure disposable income? I'll bet very few. Then again, I could be wrong.

Still- If I could only have one magazine subscription, this would be it.

text: I don't know about you, but I buy science/engineering magazines for science/engineering articles-pretty crazy, huh?  When I received the latest issue with a cover of Joe Biden and his son, I had to wonder what the relevance was.  Could it have anything to do with an election that is 6 months away, hmmm.  If I want to read a publication with a political bias, there are many to choose from; I want to read about science and related fields and Popular Science is not the forum to discuss political figures and ideology.  Not that Popular Mechanicics is the only technical publication that does it; Popular Science had a cover with President Obama just a month or two ago.  And no, I do not want to see an article about Donald Trump.  I do NOT want to see articles about ANY political figures.  So it is for this reason I have cancelled subscriptions to both of these publications, I do not feel the publishers for these magazines should be promoting a political agenda under the guise of a "feel good" story when their intent is to achieve a political goal.

title: Just what she wanted!
text:
What a refreshing relief! My 13-year-old daughter loves it. I am so happy---I loved Seventeen when I was a teen and read it voraciously for years! But it has certainly changed! Back in the day (looooong time ago), Seventeen didn't run articles about sexual positions and detailed info about contracting STDs and birth control. I'm no prude, but I know my daughter and she isn't dealing with any of this yet and doesn't need or want this information, and it is forced on her EVERYWHERE---in the media, at school, everywhere. It is just so sad how young girls are hypersexualized at such young ages even by forces considering themselves proactive do-gooders. This magazine is for the teenager who wants to know about fashion, beauty, fitness and what's trendy in movies (PG-13--yes!), music (young women artists--yes!) and books (lots of women authors--yes!) for young people. I'm not jazzed about the massive amount of advertising and products, but that's standard in women's publishing, so if you can get past all that, this celebrates diversity and creativity in girls and is very upbeat and fun. Nice work, Justeen LLC.

If you are looking for something more serious, intellectual and not beauty/fashion/ad focused, I would recommend New Moon Girls magazine also. It is much more expensive, though, of course, because it is not subsidized by advertisers.

text:
Car and Driver is the magazine that I turn to when I want to know the real story behind a car. Some of their compeititor magazines, claim to be about cars, but then all I find inside are cars that I will never see in America and that I couldn't afford if I did find one.

Car and Driver was made to talk to the people of America who aspire to pay a lot of money to drive something that is better than our rusting Geo Metro's. Their pictures and poetic words tell stories of the better life. The life where we all drive 3-Series BMW's or where we take our Shelby Cobra's to the track for the weekend. Yet they also acknowledge and relate to the fact that most of us drive to and from work with a large number of french fries lying below our seats.

While this magazine might not be enough to defeat sharks with freaking lasers; I can promise you that it will be enough to make you an educated consumer and dreamer. You will learn to wait by the mail box eagerly awaiting your monthly fix like myself and every other happy subscriber.

title: Bold, fact-based, satirical political mag that has it all
text:
I've tried a lot of different political magazines and, so far, Current Affairs has been the best.

Fact based and unabashedly honest reporting from journalists who put the interests of people before those of the extraordinarily wealthy and corporations. This magazine is a refreshing change from mainstream corporate political magazines which, by nature of their owners/funding sources, are hesitant to unwilling to publish critiques that actually challenge the status quo. The journalists that write for Current Affairs take a critical and unyielding look at mainstream narratives and offer fact-based perspectives on their accuracy, origins, and implications, using satire and comedy to make for an enjoyable reading experience.

If you're looking for a news source that's not afraid to speak truth to power, you've come to the right place.

title: High Ticket Price Is Justified!
text:
If you are a fan of a certain genre of music,be it mainstream pop, punk or hip-hop, there are at least a few magazines to cater to your taste. The rarity is a magazine that caters to the all-around pop music fanatic, and Mojo Magazine tops that obscure list.

This is a pricey publication, but well worth the money. Since discovering the magazine several years ago, I have been amazed at the diversity in the cover features alone: The Beatles, ABBA, Frank Zappa, Kate Bush, The White Stripes, Michael Jackson, Rolling Stones, Sex Pistols, Madonna... there is something for everybody's taste, and plenty for people with a wide range of musical taste.

Cover features inside, I am always amazed at the space they give to performers and/or bands that have a small cult following. I especially enjoyed the piece they did on The Incredible String Band several years back. As they usually do when covering a group's history, the Mojo writers do not shy away from the friction and low points involved in the band's career. No tabloid trash-talking or finger pointing, just good solid journalism; showing the strengths that makes an icon's popularity endure, and the bumps in the road that ended the ride.

The reviews of CDs are plenty, and I often find myself discovering something new to add to my collection. You'll find reviews of pop, punk, folk, blues, country, classic rock, you name it! I also find the reviewers to be a lot more open minded when reviewing albums, which is a welcome holiday from the plethora of snobbish music critics who go out of their way to trash good efforts.

Mojo, in my humble opinion, is top of the music mags. If you are an over all pop-culture fan like I am, and are always on the lookout for something new to add to your collection, then Mojo Magazine should be a key resource in your database!

title: Confused editors add "political science" to Scientific American
text:
It matters not whether Scientific American has adopted a political leaning that can be described as "liberal" - the decision to pull politics into its pages is enough in itself to turn off many longtime readers. To those who say to this frustrated group "maybe you people just can't wrap your head around the science" -- No! So many of these reviews come from people who would love to wrap their heads around actual science, they're just having a hard time finding it in Scientific American.

In 1990, a Scientific American article on climate change talked about the science of climate change. Observations. Patterns. Theories. Compare Wally Broecker's "What Drives Glacial Cycles" to something you might find today. Sadly, a once great magazine has traded explanations of vertical mixing patterns, astronomical cycles, and meltwater theories for this kind of crap:

Casualties of Climate Change
Scientific American (January 2011), 304, 64-71
(available free: [...])

...a seven page summary of predictions with no actual discussion of the underlying science. Today's Scientific American reader need not bother with such details. Today's Scientific American reader need only know that smart people are studying the problem and, that although the outlook isn't good, there *is* something that the *rest of us* can do "to alleviate the inevitable suffering" caused by global warming. Simply refer to Box 3, "Policy Implications" for a well-thought out list of achievable goals to present to policymakers. The first suggestion is "reduce greenhouse gas emissions to safe levels" - yes, really. I mean, if we're going to go there, let's put "world peace" on the list. I'm sure that would help, too.

I'm poking fun in part to point out that one of the problems with this article is that it's written by scientists. After all, most scientists are no better at politics than most politicians are at science.

I love science. But I could care less about what political position some writer or editor advocates. So long as Scientific American runs with the idea that "science and politics are inextricably intertwined" I'll be running elsewhere for information.

After a long day of answering phones at work, I don't want my home phone to ring. But NatGeo will call, they will call again, sometimes they'll just hang up on you, sometimes they'll pitch a product.
With many print publications dying off due to the internet, it's amazing that NatGeo is driving customers away by becoming a 400 lb gorilla.

"Acoustic Guitar" publisher:  There is simply too much quality competition out there in the marketplace for you to permit sloppy business practices. title: Not worth the price
text:
I love design magazines. I love to read about design and watch it on TV. I was ready to love Fresh Home. But this magazine is simply a failure and not worth the cost.

I originally got this magazine as a freebie offer-- one I forgot about for the longest time because it took so long to get it. When it finally came, that first issue was pretty good. It was good enough that even though they were harassing me telling me I needed to pay for a full year subscription since I received my free copy (they threatened to send me to collections only a week or two after I received the issue because they required you then buy the magazine after receiving the free preview) I decided to pay the $10 and subscribe.

From there the magazine got worse. For one, they have several design articles without any sort of photos or buying guide. Most are just writers talking about their ideas of design with no visuals or proof to back it up. For example, how can you have a more than two page story about how to cheaply decorate an apartment with no photos, product suggestions, etc? They also overly use clip art to fill in for their lack of photos. Most come off as juvenile and unnecessary. The articles come off more has filler for the ads than content to help the reader. A recent article about your garden design style has clip art and one photo of an example garden. It included no explanation for what the design or plants in the gardens were. The best it gave if you seeking designing a garden to suit your style was a list of flowers, followed by what music you like if you fit their cliché description and what clothes you wear. ??? How is that design? How does this help my home?

I am not sure after a year of reading (with magazines only coming about once every 3 months) who their audience is? Some sections include how to make a cheap table out of plywood and then they suggest backyard furniture with the cheapest chair costing $600. Is it the poor 20-something or the rich house wife who has nothing better to do than build cheap tables and buy overpriced furniture? In terms of design, there is no clear theme and the articles lack visuals to help people interested in design bring the ideas into their home.

On top of the poor writing, the editors are continually begging for your money. On the front of one magazine was a phrase "Buy this magazine or we'll have to put this dog up for adoption." Apparently the dog in the shoot was owned by an editor. Attached to every magazine-- despite my recent sign-up for a full year of Fresh Home-- was a letter begging me to renew my subscription, pointing out the hardship of print media in today's economic times and the cost for the magazine to keep sending me letters to subscribe. Well if it costs so much to send the letters, then stop sending them! Especially when I just signed up! Frankly as someone who works in the print industry as a journalist, I found all this in poor taste, adding to my overall dislike of the magazine.

It's a new magazine so I was willing to give them a chance to find their footing, but the cost and juvenile writing is not worth it when you can get sure-bet design mags monthly for half the cost. Save your money and buy Better Homes and Gardens or House Beautiful.

Plus at parties you'll know all about the devaluation of the Argentine Peso, the dangers of EMT, The arguments about drilling for oil in the Artic. The latest scoop on the war against terrorism.
Ever since Ms. Brown took over the reins (and has since left) the writing has tightened up, fewer words, more meaning. Turns out past authors were paid by the number of words printed, so for a highly expensive well researched article, editors and authors would slyly conspire to pay the author by letting them ramble on. To the detriment of the reader. Now that system seems to be by the wayside as the duplicate paragraphs are gone and yet the quality of the research is still great.
If you don't subscribe to the Sunday NYTimes, get this. Or drop the sunday edition and get just the daily, and subscribe to this. The writing is better, the subject matter wider. Great value in $/per page worth reading.

title: Used to be a great magazine; cancelling my 25+ year subscription!
text: I have subscribed to InStyle for well over 25 years. I LOVED this magazine. Frankly, I'm annoyed at reading the same word over and over again, month after month:  Badass. They have latched onto a word and run wild with it. How can people want to read the same thing over and over again? I feel it's juvenile. If you have to point out that you are badass, you are not badass. LOL. In the past few years with the newest editor, especially the last year, InStyle has become little more than a one-sided political blog and a one-sided feminist publication. There are two sides to every story and the view that InStyle is putting out is a narrow one. That's fine for those who agree with InStyle's message, but I like to hear all sides. I am a woman and think women are great and I value other women, but it's over the top. Not every issue needs to state that women are "badass" just because they made something of themselves. There are occasional stories about women who are making a difference in the world in a positive manner, or truly doing something remarkable, but most of them seem to be just pushing their own personal agendas and/or are just fluff. I find it very hard to believe that all these actresses and politicians use the term "badass" in their conversation as much as InStyle would have us believe (in order to justify their use of the word). Boy, is the word badass watered down for me now. LOL. Not to mention I don't really care for reading some of the stories with the F-word. I suppose some people find that refreshing in some way, but I personally don't care for it. Where I have seen it, it has seemed to be just put there for shock value alone. Surely, these intelligent, educated and beautiful women can get their ideas across without being a potty-mouth on the written page. InStyle has become a smaller and smaller magazine with almost no fashion sense. I decided today was my issue when I felt ridiculous spending my time reading badass this and badass that, to the point where I lost count. There was no page with the contact info and no info other than the editor was given. Has InStyle shut down any letters to the editor or responses to articles from their readers? It was not even identified who the publisher is. Very odd. All that to say, I am very sorry that the old InStyle, a fashion and home magazine that was fun to read on a Saturday morning, has very little to do with fashion anymore. Perhaps it should be renamed, "Badass." Ha, ha.

title: Mere shadow of the publication that it once was.  Also they renew without permission
text:
First, it had been many years since I saw a copy of this magazine. My mother had a subscription going all the way back to the 1950's, my grandmother had a subscription going back to her own childhood. My mother inherited all her mothers copies when my grandmother died. I inherited those going back to February 1922, just over 1000 issues. I still have them. I have since read every issue. I hadn't read it in years, not since the late 1970's. I was missing 2007-2020 and figured I could catch up at the public library. I saw it advertised here on Amazon in 2020 and felt nostalgic so I ordered a one year subscription for $5. I got about $5 worth. It is unfortunate that the publishers have decided to reduce the Wallace's masterpiece into something for people with short attention spans. To say I was disappointed is an understatement. The magazine is 1/4 the size I remember and it shrunk from a monthly subscription to ten times a year. I decided not to renew.

In the autumn of 2021 I continued to receive issues past my one year subscription date. I took the issue back to the post office with a note attached telling them to cancel. I continued to get issues and have repeated this every time they sent an issue since. I was just reviewing my account and discovered a charge for $17.98 for a renewal and Amazon told me they could not cancel the subscription that it was too late. I checked the archive of my purchases and discovered that they slipped this by me last year and I never noticed on my checking account. I have gone from disappointed to furious. Not only have they desecrated the Wallace's masterpiece but they have turned it into a criminal enterprise!

I strongly recommend NOT ordering this subscription. If your local library has this magazine archived I suggest going there and reading copies from prior to this century. The worst article from before 2000 is infinitely better than the best one I read in the one year of subscription that I authorized.

One final note. They are no longer publishing 10 issues a year. If you order this and expect 10 issues you will be disappointed. This magazine is now only published 9 times a year. And while it always had advertising, it is now more than 50% advertising which is another extreme disappointment.

Naturally, grilling is the "haute cuisine" on this auspicious day. The recipes for "Salmon Nicoise Sandwiches" and "Tuscan Baby Back Ribs" are mouth-watering ...

The "fast food" section is loaded with tasty healthful salads, such as, "Spicy Chicken, Avacado, and Mango Salad" and "Turkey and Green Bean Stir-Fry with Peanuts". Some grilling suggestions include, "Tandoori Pork with Gingered Mango Salad" and "Korean-Style Chicken Wraps". Needless to say, all the food is tempting and the recipes are not too difficult to accomplish, provided one is already familiar with cooking techniques.

Overall, the emphasis on this magazine is *not* on wine but instead on food. For a change of pace, the June issue has a very fine article on "vodka". In the July 2004 issue there is a superb article by Robert Parker called, "Australian Wine Guide". The regular wine column covers "German Reisling" by Richard Nailey. Most impressively, the July issue introduces the reader to "America's Best New Chefs of 2004". Of course, each selects a recipe to share. This magazine is loaded with unique articles for the adventurous cook and aspiring gourmand. Highly recommended. Erika Borsos (erikab93)

title: Analogy
text:
Wine Spectator is to wine knowledge as
Playboy pictorials are to real sex.

Now that I have your attention.

The wine industry needs a glossy, and the Wine Spectator is it. If you want to be a wine geek, subscribe to International Wine Cellar or Wine Advocat and haunt (read: drink with) the underpaid staff at your local wine merchant.

But if you want to swan around and be able to read the three and four-digit price list of a wine list and menu, then by all means make sure you memorize what is featured in the Wine Spectator.

But big glossies help everybody. First, it helps the industry, and when the industry is healthy, then the wine-geek bottles are numerous. Remember the collapse of world wine prices and France turning otherwise good grapes into vinegar and grain alcohol? Small terroir obscure producers of hand crafted approaches are the ones *most* hit by a weak industry. So yes! Bring on the yuppies reading the slick!!!

Second, sure the reviews are gushing, but the cold fact of nature is a lot of the wines featured here are supurb and if you do get your hands on them you'll enjoy them, even without the tasting notes featured here.

Third, to its credit, Wine Spectator pays attention to new world wines with the same attention and care (perhaps more so to California Cabs) the old world wines get. For decades all anyone (including Parker) wrote about was France France France. Wine Spectator started saying "hey, American Cabs are good!" and suddenly, Italian, Spanish, Chilean, Argentinean, Australian, etc. wines were getting better coverage from all thoughtful corners. This was a net good thing (although Wine Spectator has criminally neglected Austrian whites).

Forth, if wine criticism was just wine geeks and offset printed newsletters the wine world would be as sad a place as an Original Series Star Trek convention. I like a big tent where bluffing yuppies get to drink with scruffy obsessives. Sure the scruffy obsessive has sacrificed his life and economic position for the obscurity of his passion, but heck, he gets to taste bottles he would not dream of because some Wine Spectator subscriber happens to come to the geek fest.

Still, two stars because you just feel dirty that it exists.

title: Helpful, thoughtful, but skewed and human
text:
Okay, a four star review.

The Wine Advocat is a valuable newsletter written by experts and helps you save money and time buying better wines by rating and reviewing wines with an understandable and sometimes personal vocabulary and a rating on a 100-point scale.

Anyone who has ever had a test graded on a 100 point scale knows it is successful and accurate at assessing your knowledge of something *most* of the time, but not *all* of the time. The "precision" is over-fitted, but the "capture" of information is pretty accurate.

Why this is a controversial revelation to the wine-crybabies is a mystery to me. The 100 point scale is a useful hermeneutic tool, not perfect, but better than what went before it (read English wine critics of the 1920s and 30s for some real codswallop, Salvador Dali couldn't have written more bizarre prose).

There is an admitted cultus around Robert M. Parker, Officier de la Légion d'honneur, of which there are legions of fans. Well deserved, for Parker has saved lots of people lots of time with his reviews and point system.

But I don't blame Robert Parker for those who *misuse* his system and then throw stones at him. The difference between an 89 and a 90? Nothing. Time of day, particular bottle, a dirty glass, etc. When I was young and poor I only bought Parker rated 85 to 89 wines, and learned a tremendous amount about wine very cheaply. The minute a wine gets a 90 or above rating, kiss the price skyward.

So The Wine Advocat is an excellent tool, and a value, for those who are going to buy serious wine. Is Parker, Schildknecht, et. al. always right? Yes, he is always right according to his lights. Is he skewed? Yes. In the early days he liked fleshy, sweet, full bodied, overwhelming jammy red fruit wines (like Beaux Freres tastes). His handful of 99 and 100 point wines are trockenberrinauslese. Okay, so we know what the man likes.

The trick is to know what *YOU* like and then use his and his excellent writers voluminous tasting and screening to save you money and time. The Wine Advocat does that and is a value-added product.

There is an unhelpful and unfair entry on "Controversy" in Paker's online reference material. Most of them are petty beyond belief, and personal (his goddaughter? that is low, and anyone complaining about his ethics over that should be dueled to death in dishonor). But the two most unfair are about Andy Bassin's MacArthur Liquor, and most egregious David Schildknecht.

Andy Bassin's MacArthur Liquor is a great store with knowledgeable staff, the wine world is a small place, and Parker's newsletter helpful. The idea that it is wrong to try and reach that client base AND HELP THEM with a cheap newsletter is absurd. Nobody forced Bassin's clients to subscribe to The Wine Advocat, they aren't zombies, they are people with free will.

The scurrilous "controversy" over David Schildknecht is more shameful. Most folks working in wine struggle to make a living. Think how hard it is to be a wine expert in an industry where *rich*people*do*it*for*free*and*can*afford*things*you*can't*. Enter the "controversy" of David Schildknecht writing as a wine critic while also trying to make a living importing and selling wine.

There just isn't one. David Schildknecht is one of the hardest working, smartest, well-read, thoughtful, decent, honest, intelligent, ethical, and champions of good wine that is working in the industry today. He has *never* sold me a bottle of bad wine, and he and Josh Raynolds of Stephen Tanzer's International Wine Cellar are the best writers working in the field today. The question is, who would you trust on their opinion, someone who is independently wealthy and just importing mountains of plonk and three cases of superb wine, and flogging it off on an unsuspecting army of zombies? Or David who makes his living and reputation off wine and wine alone. David, Josh, Tanzer, and Parker win hands down any day.

If you can only subscribe to one wine newsletter then I'd subscribe to Stephen Tanzer's The International Wine Cellar, but if you have money for both then get The Wine Advocat too for complete coverage.

Four stars to emphasize that you shouldn't become a Parker zombie or greasy-haired, medallion wearing, leisure-suited Wine Spectator poseur.

title: USED TO BE BETTER
text:
I have been a subscriber for years and have grudgingly paid more and more every year for my subscription. Still I have always loved PW and look forward to my weekly edition...although I do not always receive my magazine in a timely manner. Whether because I live on the West Coast or if it's just the mail, I don't know. Sometimes it arrives way into the following week, sometimes closer to the beginning of the week. I still find the magazine valuable, but have to say the following:

For a magazine directed at the publishing trade I find it ludicrous that there are so many typos in the reviews as well as the text. WHO IS DOING THE PROOF READING HERE? There is a new format that has updated the look, but I miss the best seller lists being in the back of the magazine. Now they're somewhat in the middle and one definitely can't just easily flip to them. Also, the Q&A's with authors are so stupidly placed in issues which don't contain the review of the author's book who is being interviewed. Instead, there is a reference date to the issue said book was reviewed in. It's frustrating to read the Q&A and then not be able to see the review of the author's book in the same issue. I guess the publisher thinks people keep the magazine at least 4 weeks or issues just lie around the house or office and pile up. I like the "Deals" columm and "Hollywood Reader" column, but my very favorite section is the Author Profile. I am curious tho about the age of some of the writers in this publication... I'd also like to know how the magazine and the editors decide what book should get a starred review. Sometimes I'm astounded as to what gets starred. The website, which you get full access to when you register as a subscriber to the magazine, is easy to use. Even before I receive my issue in the mail, I can see the latest issue on line.

title: A great magazine
text:
This is one of the most fun food magazines I have ever come across. It has plenty of good recipes that are relatively accessible to the average cook, but it also has lots of articles that are both informative & entertaining.

The primary focus (of course) is on hot and spicy foods, but it also concentrates on any number of regional cuisines that are not necessarily scorching hot. A issue highlighting salsas, for example, will have a fair number of high-Scoville recipes, but will also include flavorful salsas that are intended to enhance a main course rather bring beads of sweat to your forehead. A neophyte will better understand that a salsa isn't necessarily a hot sauce but actually covers a much wider spectrum. The same would apply to their issues on barbeque as well as cuisines from Mexico, Thailand & India, among others.

If you want to know how to grow peppers, you will also find this magazine informative, as it addresses many different aspects of pepper horticulture. There is also plenty of information on the frighteningly extensive array of hot sauces that are commercially available. If you come from a region where it isn't easy to grow your own peppers, finding a resource for peppers is important, and this magazine definitely helps.

Even if you aren't a pepper-head, there is plenty within this magazine that you will find useful.

It has great virtual trips - like to Thailand, Oaxaco, and Jamaica woven around the theme of the liquid pleasures produced in each country - everything from tea to rum, or chocolate. title: How Do I Know Which Magazine To Buy?
text:
So, you are interested in astronomy and ready to pick up a subsciption to an astronomy magazine, but are not sure which magazine to purchase? First let me say, "Good for you!" I never go a month without a magazine. It is difficult to keep up to date with the night sky without a monthly guide.

But you are probably trying to decide whether to read "Astronomy" magazine or "Sky & Telescope". These are the two big North American competitors. The good news is, you won't go wrong. Both are excellent magazines and both are of similar quality, size, and usefullness. I regularly read both of them. The difference is a matter of subtle leaning. Astronomy magazine leans a little more toward the amateur. It includes monthly selections that will help a person who is learning the sky. It is a favorite of those who appreciate the beauty of the night sky. Sky & Telescope is a little more technical. It is written for someone who tackles the subject with the passion of a scholar. As I wrote, the difference is subtle. Either way, you won't go wrong.

Let me go out on a limb here. If you are reading this review and trying to decide, you probably will enjoy Astronomy magazine more.

UNLESS . . .

That is, unless you do not own a telescope and do own a pair of binoculars. Sky & Telescope includes a small "Binocular Highlight". It isn't large, less than a page, but it is enough to challenge you.

Which way do I personally lean? Last year I leaned toward Sky & Telescope and picked up occasional Astronomy magazines at the bookstore. This year I subscribe to Astronomy and pick up occasional Sky & Telescopes at the books store. Next year . . .who knows? I keep trying out different magazines and comparing them. I also subscribe to another astronomy magazine.

A final word, there are other serious contenders in the field of astronomy magazines. For example, "Sky at Night" has them both beat, but it costs a lot more, so I don't get it.

title: The Choice of 'Mugwumps' Forevermore
text:
The venerable Atlantic Monthly has always been professedly 'moderate', a stance that in today's political spectrum is a euphemism for conservative. Since it abandoned proper Boston for flashy DC, the magazine has tried hard to shake its reputation for being staid and stuffy, chiefly by becoming fashionably shallow while yet implying an insider's right to posture as 'above the fray.' Such was the posture of Henry Adams, too pure of mind to take politics seriously during Reconstruction. Such was the self-admiring posture of the Mugwump faction of the 19th C GOP, with its mug on one side of the fence and its 'wump' on the other. As other reviewers have already declared, the Atlantic can and often does make any subject boring. It's a magazine I often pick up in waiting rooms and airport book stores but would never choose to subscribe to.

However!!! The December 2009 issue contained an article titled "Did Christianity Cause the Crash? How Preachers are Spreading a Gospel of Debt" by Hanna Rosin, an article that no one could possibly regard as timorous or equivocal. Specifically, Rosin has investigated the role the 'prosperity gospel', preached by some ministers of fundamentalist Christianity, played in the Bush II real estate bubble and the subsequent economic depression. That some of said ministers had their own financial links to sleazy-easy mortgages is not terribly surprising, is it? This is an article well worth reading, even if you conclude that Rosin is talking through her hat -- not my conclusion, I assure you -- and one that should have gotten more circulation than the shrinking readership of the Atlantic provides.

title: A TV Show on Paper
text:
DISCOVER has positioned itself somewhere halfway between "Nature" and "People" magazines. There are still fine, lucid, informative articles, though not in every issue, but there are also ill-written inadequately fact-checked blurts. If your basic scientific fund of knowledge is broad enough, you'll have no trouble ignoring the latter. More annoying for me are the occasional feature articles that slither into science-fantasy, that suggest serious professional interest in flimsy fly-by-night notions.

Nevertheless, I subscribe. I even pick it up at kiosks when I'm on the road and I miss an issue. It's not a big investment of reading time -- scarcely a flight from Minneapolis to Montreal worth -- and precisely because it's mere pop journalism, it's less infuriating than Scientific American.

title: More Poultry News for your Money!
text:
The Poultry Press has been delivering the goods on purebred poultry for many generations, with the youngest member of the latest generation beginning to learn the process. This is no "fly by night" rag, and you'll always be a winner when you receive your monthly issue. And if you are a big fan of Purina poultry feeds, you'll get more than your subscription rate returned by using the valuable coupons in each issue. The most prevalent is the ' $5.00 off of two bags' of poultry feed, your choice, but twice in the past few months, I've received the greater " $15.00 off of six bags of feed," which amounts to quite a savings!

The articles included in each issue range from the very easy, follow the numbers type, to the more detailed uses of genetics in developing more from your birds. There is something here for each level of poultry enthusiast, with valuable medical advice, friendly "how-to's" for those of us who may not know how-to, and an easy to read format, even for those of us who must use those all important "readers!"

Plus, the family who runs the Poultry Press have been diligent in giving of their time, their service, and their financial help to the many quality shows they cover each year. They travel from one end of our continent to the other, to make sure their readers receive the very latest in poultry news, from new laws and regulations to the latest breakthroughs in the purebred poultry industry.

You'll find available, qualified judges in one section, ranked breed clubs in another, and news about the 'Future of the Fancy,' as co-owner Bill Wulff calls our young folks.

You can't go wrong with this one, this is one fine egg!

Yours in the Fancy,
Sandy

title: I used to love it. Now, not so much.
text:
I used to love Entertainment Weekly. I started subscribing in the early '90s and would read it cover-to-cover each week. Then in the 2000s, it became increasingly political. At first it was little comments and digs here and there. Then it gradually became more aggressive. A few years ago I finally gave up and cancelled my subscription and never looked back. The final straw was when they viciously attacked a celebrity who made a politically incorrect statement that the editors did NOT like. This from the magazine that gave the Dixie Chicks the cover after their offensive remarks, letting them wrap themselves in the 1st Amendment, and which lectured its readers on the need for tolerance and willingness to hear opposing views. I agree with those principles and was disgusted at how selectively this magazine chose to follow them. It seems everything is getting politicized these days and it would have been nice for EW to have been a fun little non-political oasis. On those occasions when the entertainment world intersected with politics, maybe cover it without taking sides.

To be honest, that's not the only reason I quit EW. I had also grown tired of all the fawning publicity puff pieces. Journalist meets Celebrity at a restaurant. Journalist details what Celebrity wore (so stylish!). The two discuss Celebrity's latest project with a breezy air, as though they're the best of friends. Celebrity laughs in response to Journalist's clever question. Journalist is impressed at how cool Celebrity is. You really must read/watch Celebrity's latest book/movie/TV show... On the plus side, the reviews section was usually pretty good.

While I stopped reading it, I continue to give it as a gift subscription to my sister, who still enjoys it.

text:
I was looking for a magazine to get a friend's teenage daughter who is at an age where she is interested in pop stars, beauty tips, fashion, celebrity news with a tasty bite, a bit of serious writing to make her think; after all she is at an age where she has to face the real world.

My friend's daughter is mixed race and though I think she would like Seventeen from a girly point of view, I do think she will find it hard at times to identify with, because it does come across as "quite white."

All the same it is a good magazine; it has well written articles, good photography and knows how to target its audience.

All the same I will be giving it a miss on a subscription level for the moment as I don't think it is really suitable for someone who is not white, maybe in the future when it diversifies.

title: Vogue is so OUT of vogue
text:
A friend once said to me, "If you want a glossy that is a no brainer then get Vogue!"

How right she is, despite having glorious photography, fashion models that daren't stand sideways or you wouldn't be able to see them and the occasional good article in it, I have to admit I find Vogue too pretentious.

Vogue wants to be the voice of fashion, the voice of the high brow media but its clientele are the likes of you and me, ordinary people who can't afford to live the high life they are portraying on its gloss filled pages.

Personally I'd rather spend my money on a movie ticket, I get to see a good thriller, sci-fi, romance etc, etc I don't have to know about the substence abuse and emotional demons that haunt a particular actor's life, I'm just interested in enjoying myself for a couple of hours before I go back to my hard working life in the real world.

Vogue is trying to sell me a dream that I don't really want to buy into, never had a penchant for selling my soul to the devil, it's gets two stars though because the photography is really superb, shame about the rest of it though.

I was quite impressed, it was well written and quite unbiased, rare in a magazine that is known for its skinny models/actors/musicians who lounge elegantly as they give interviews whilst looking the camera and say in hot sultry voices, "Darling, I'm an artist, it's my passion, my love, that's why I do it!"

I won't say that Vanity Fair has given me too much food for thought but it has been enough for me to take out a year's subscription to see if they can come up with anything else that is remotely intelligent and thoughtful and they haven't done too badly up to now.

title: Looks Like They've Gone Down In Quality (and Quantity) From a Few Years Ago....
text:
I subscribed to GW for years and years, until I was informed a few years ago that they had decided to go to all digital subscriptions and would no longer be providing print copies to subscribers.

After writing and telling them there's no way subscribers are going to sit at their computer screens and read through a 60 page magazine each month, I got a response back saying, essentially, too bad. When I wrote back saying they'd be forced to bring back print subscriptions because too many subscribers would cancel rather than be forced to go to a digital only subscription, and I still had like 4 months left on my subscription and I had paid for a print subscription, I got a note back saying they would pro rate my account, cancel my subscription, and send me a check. I received a check in the mail a week or so later for $4. As you can imagine, I did not appreciate the treatment I received from them at all.

Recently, I saw that they had, in fact, brought back print subscriptions, so I went to a Barnes & Noble and checked out a copy. I was surprised to find the magazine is noticeably thinner than it had previously been, there's ads on nearly every page, there was not one article that I was interested in reading, and the tabs were all for songs in Drop D tuning, which I do not play... at all. That heavy death metal stuff does not interest me at all.

Being a guitarist for over 45 years now, I'm always looking to stay in touch with equipment, technique, the latest groups, current releases and so on, so I'll keep tabs on GW going forward. It used to be a "must have" magazine, as far as I was concerned, for many years. Not so much from what I've seen of the issue I checked out, but it's good to see they've gone back to offering print subscriptions once again. I'll keep my eye out when I visit B&N going forward, but they certainly appear to have gone downhill from what they were before.

title: Visually Impaired Readers??
text:
I have problems with the content of RD compared with years ago, but that’s not my chief complaint.

Amazon offers these prices for RD: print-$5.00 Kindle-$.99
READER’S DIGEST LARGE PRINT EDITION— $22.00 ??!!

A 250% increase for a visually impaired person? That’s unconscionable!! Think about it. Yes, there are software programs and technology to aid in reading and other tasks when impaired. But those are very expensive for the average person.

There are many ways that the cost of the magazine can be offset before charging the consumer so much. The same software and technologies can make the actual printing a very simple process. There may be a somewhat higher cost for paper, but not this much!

There are grants, both state and federal, that magazines and Amazon can apply for that will help decrease this cost. But for heaven's sake! Doesn’t Amazon make enough money to OFFER SIMILAR GRANTS TO LOWER THE COST OF MATERIALS TO BLIND AND VISUALLY IMPAIRED READERS??

(I think so, because they offer so many periodicals at $5.00.)

I don’t know what other magazines have done this, but I will go look. I’m an advocate for Visually Impaired people, and was a Vision teacher for many years. This is very disheartening.

title: Not As Good As it Used to Be
text:
I have been a faithful subscriber to RS for almost twenty years, and I have witnessed the magazine slowly transform from a credible rock and roll journal to the music equivilent of Tiger Beat. In the 1980s, Rolling Stone's passion was music, and it often gave well-deserved nods to artists that were on the cutting edge: U2, Prince, REM, the Smiths, and so on. These days, its attempts to sell copies are getting more desperate as they feature people like Britney, NSYNC, and BSB on their cover sometimes as much as twice a year. I have nothing against teen pop; after all, RS gave Duran Duran a cover story in the 1980s. But it's troubling to see a magazine follow trends when they used to create them.
The record reviews are, for the most part, dubious. Rob Sheffield is one of the usual suspects. Three-and-a-half stars for Britney and Destiny's Child? More trustworthy critics include longtime writer David Fricke, Anthony DeCurtis, and Barry Walters. These guys seem to know what they're talking about when they review records.
The only section of the magazine worth reading is the movies section by Peter Travers, a critic I may not always agree with but one I do respect. Travers has enough heart to go against the grain of public opinion by trashing shallow, self-important, corporate driven, Holllywood movies. It really seems that he is criticizing the very hype machine the rest of Rolling Stone seems to embrace.
All in all, RS has its moments, but its getting disappointing within recent years. Here's hoping it can regain the edge it once had back in the 1970s and 1980s.

title: Anti-Trump Liberal Bias
text:
Update on March 10, 2017: Once again I'm changing my rating, this time to 2 stars. Also I cancelled my subscription a few months ago. Political bias (anti-Trump, pro-Clinton) is obvious in at least 2 issues of RD: July/Aug 2016, p.96-100, "Which Way Do I Vote?"; Nov 2016, p.102-111, "Who They Really Are."

Update on Jan 25, 2016: I'm changing my rating of Reader's Digest (again) because I no longer feel that it deserves 5 stars. I'm torn between 3 and 4 stars, but will be generous (for now) and give it a 4 stars because it continues to feature some good articles and I like its handy size.

What is downgrading the magazine for me is the proliferation of ads and articles for diet books written by RD editor-in-chief, Liz Vaccariello. Liz Vaccariello has written a multitude of diet books and cookbooks in recent years--at least 7 diet books and at least 5 cookbooks. (If you think I'm exaggerating the number of her books, look her up on Amazon.) What I don't like is that she regularly promotes her books in Reader's Digest, with frequent ads and articles. Apparently she did the same thing when she was editor of Prevention Magazine, but I was never a regular reader of that magazine, so I don't know much about that. Also Prevention is a diet and exercise magazine, unlike RD.

The Feb 2016 issue of RD features an article on Liz's latest diet book. There were also 3 ads for same book in that issue--1 inside the article, another elsewhere in the magazine, and the other on the back of the mailing address card. I wouldn't complain about this if it were a rare event, but it's not: Liz's diet books are regularly promoted and advertised in RD. Being the editor of a high-circulation magazine gives her a great advertising advantage, no doubt. It's a sweet deal for her, but I find her continuous self-promotion to be annoying (and obviously very biased).

By the way, is there any evidence that her diet books work long-term? I'd love to see an article in Reader's Digest titled "Secrets Diet Book Authors Won't Tell You", but I won't hold my breath on that. I don't care how much weight Liz or her staff and friends claim they lost on her latest diet after following it for days, weeks, or a few months. I won't be impressed until there is proof that the weight loss is being maintained long-term by many. As we have all heard countless times, strong evidence indicates that the great majority of people regain whatever weight they lost on any given diet within 1-5 years. And their health often declines in the process. And it's not their fault, either: Diets (including those promoted as simple, easy, and healthy) are generally complicated, unpleasant (for the dieter and their families), costly, and are not realistically sustainable long-term. But regardless of the quality or effectiveness or lack thereof, I am simply tired of seeing Liz's diets promoted so often.

As someone else mentioned: Since my 2014 update, RD went back to 10 issues per year. The decrease in issues doesn't bother me as long as the expiration dates don't mysteriously change as they did a few years ago. On a positive note, RD is now including digital access with each subscription. While I don't plan to take advantage of that myself, it's an added value which I expect will be popular with many readers.

Update on Aug 18, 2014: My original review below was written almost 2 years ago. I'm happy to say that there have been many improvements since then, so I now need to update my review and change my rating from 1 star to 5 stars. Everything I complained about in my original review has been corrected! The magazine continues to publish occasional "mature" jokes, but on a mild level--nothing offensive like that dirty joke about the Easter Bunny. There are now 12 issues per year (1 per month) with no more confusing and changeable expiration dates. Another improvement: the number of ads was actually reduced. Also the quality of the magazine's paper has improved. No more thin, slippery paper; now the paper is thicker and whiter, which makes it easy on the eyes as well as easy to turn the pages. Best of all, the articles have significantly improved! Lately every issue has been full of interesting, informative, and heartwarming articles. My congratulations and thanks to editor Liz Vaccariello and the other staff for all these great improvements. I very happily resubscribed to Reader's Digest!

Original Review (Nov. 15, 2012): Until recently Reader's Digest had all-clean jokes. You could read all the jokes out loud to your children or grandchildren of any age. No more. Page 110 of the September 2012 issued featured a joke about the Easter Bunny having sex with a chicken. Isn't that a great joke for your children and grandchildren? This joke didn't accidentally sneak into the magazine. They knew the joke was dirty, which is why it was titled "Favorite joke I can't share with my kid." In another comedy section on page 121 of the same issue, you get to see an x-ray of a man that has sunglasses up his rectum (due to accidentally sitting on them). Not exactly family-friendly humor.

Many customers (myself included) wrote to editor Liz Vaccariello (she became editor in 2011) to complain. In the Letters section of the November 2012 issue, Ms. Vaccariello apologized for the "off-color joke" about the Easter Bunny (which she calls "a rabbit") and said, "Please know it won't happen again." Yet in that very same November issue there are additional off-color jokes. For example, on page 160, there's a joke about a woman who punches her husband for "25 years of bad sex" and he punches her back for "knowing the difference."

I'll mention something else new (in the past couple of years) that I don't like about the magazine: the expiration dates keep changing. Occasionally they put out what they call a "special" issue, which they count as 2 issues. When this happens, your expiration date automatically changes. If at first it expires in May, then it's changed to April, then to March. On and on it goes and it's even more annoying when it involves a gift subscription. Let's say you give a subscription to a friend for a Christmas gift. You paid for "one year" and expect your friend to receive issues from Jan 2013 through Dec 2013. Well, that won't happen because there will probably be 2 "special" issues during 2013. In that event, your friend's subscription will automatically be changed to expire with the Oct 2013 issue. Of course, Reader's Digest will start bugging you to renew your gift subscription well before it expires. So around June, they will try to get you to renew what's supposed to be a Christmas gift. If you renew it that year, come the following year, the new expiration will likely have been changed to August. Have fun trying to keep up with Christmas gifts when you have to renew them in the summer. Reader's Digest pulls the same expiration date stunt on all the wonderful Reiman magazines (Reminisce, Country, Birds & Blooms, etc.). The Reiman magazines are still high quality, thanks to having good editors, however Reader's Digest has made some unwelcome changes to them, as well--most regrettably, the addition of ads in these formerly ad-free publications.

Well, that's it for me. Today (after subscribing for about 30 years) I cancelled my subscription to Reader's Digest.

title: If Only More People Read It
text:
On the fence about getting the Economist? It's not the cheapest subscription, is it?
Ask yourself: "Do I care about what's happening in the world, or do I only care about sports and weather?" then follow up with "Am I able to think honestly about new ideas?" "Will I make an hour a week to really dig into the interesting articles?"

If you can read and you care about what happens in the world and you are open to perhaps changing your mind when presented with factual arguments, then the Economist is for you. They aren't always right, but they are always insightful and fair. In a world so full of corporate sponsored BS that an out-of-his-league frat boy can get elected as the most powerful man on Earth (twice), its nice to find refreshing truth. Sure, The Economist is written from the viewpoint of Economists, but what do you expect? You can't accuse them of being illogical or heartless, and they certainly understand money, which is about as important as you suspect it is.

Go ahead, arm yourself with understanding. It's the only way to stay afloat. You'll get more wisdom from one cover story in The Economist than from a month of watching news-style TV stations. You will be poorer without The Economist than with it.

title: Easily the best video magazine available for the genre fanatic
text:
I've been buying "Video Watchdog" on and off for at least 15 years; in the past year I've finally succumbed to the lure of it completely and I'm glad I have. Every issue of this slick digest is a treasure-trove of serious, thoughtful (but never humorless or dry) reviewing, criticism and discussion about the wonderful worlds of science fiction, fantasy, and horror filmmaking as it appears on home video - first on VHS and laserdisc, then on DVD, now increasingly on Blu-ray. Editor and regular writer Tim Lucas has an obsessive, geeky level of detail at his command and expects the same out of others on his staff. Films are typically reviewed for both technical merits - both audio and video discussed in enough detail for most technophiles but simply enough for those of us with less interest in such things - and for their qualities as art, though in the case of very famous films like, say, 2001: A SPACE ODYSSEY in its recent Blu-ray release the technical considerations usually are the bulk of the piece.

The format typically offers "Dog Bytes" - short reviews of 200-500 words over a dozen pages or so at the beginning of the magazine and longer "DVDs" reviews ranging from about 700-2000 words near the end; Lucas also writes a 1-page editorial that often waxes philosophical or broadly political, there are book and CD (movie music usually) reviews, and in the last few years writer Ramsey Campbell has had a column that he usually devotes to something really, really obscure. Then there is the feature article, a lengthy review or interview, often in roundtable form; recent examples have been a long discussion of Dario Argento's MOTHER OF TEARS and an interview with Roger Corman about the Edgar Alan Poe adaptations he made in the 1960s.

Lest you say "but I'm not much interested in those kinds of films", the Watchdog often covers film noir, spaghetti and other westerns, classic cartoons and anime, and works of various major directors who have at least a little connection to weirdness and fantasy. You might not ever find a John Ford cover feature, but Welles, Bergman, Fellini, Tarkovsky or Godard aren't out of the question.

In short, my very favorite film magazine, and one of the few magazines I've ever read regularly cover-to-cover for years, and that has never diminished in quality.

And for those who do not know what this means -- the Imminent Return doctrine is a belief that our Lord can come at any moment, like right this second.  The Rapture doctrine is different from the Resurrection Doctrine in that it calls for TWO returns of our Lord -- one in secret and the other to take over the Earth and punish the wicked.  How this secret return is accomplished is up for a lot of speculation, after all, how can you have millions of Christians disappearing from the face of the Earth and it be a secret.  There are other objections as well.  BUT -- while I disagree with that particular doctrine, I find the magazine very informative and educational, and very forward thinking and not your typical, run of the mill Protestant rag.
