title: Just a Conservative Magazine
text:
I wanted to find a magazine that would give logical and sound libertarian analyses on our country's issues. As a left-leaning libertarian, I often find myself agreeing with some of the logic of libertarianism but find it often not very practical. I didn't expect this magazine to be very different; but at the very least I was hoping that its analyses would be firmly in the vein of libertarian thought, perhaps in the style of Judge Andrew Napolitano, without succumbing to the foolish politics of the day.

Unfortunately, I was wrong.

This magazine frequently devolves into popular partisan themes and arguments that really don't hold up. For example, there is a lot of TSA bashing; blindly favoring economic libertarianism over environmental issues (as opposed to accepting climate science and finding a libertarian solution); pro-life stances; lazy over-simplified conservative arguments (unions hinder motivation of people)... so on and so forth.

I could accept the conservative-libertarian columns of the magazine if it was balanced with some left-leaning libertarian columns. but it doesnt even do that.

In the end, this is just a conservative magazine that utilizes some libertarian arguments to justify the standard conservative platform. its not about thought, not about searching for the truth, and certainly not about reason....

title: Well...

Outdoor photography is difficult from an artistic standpoint, but from a technique standpoint there's just not all that much to know. Put your camera on a tripod when you can. Worry about Lens flare. Autofocus is good for rapidly moving animals. Wait for the light. Experiment with fill flash until you find a level that you like. Ho hum. You're not going to find any tips in this magazine on how to bring out the highlights of a B&W photo with farmer's reducer, or anything like that. It's all on the blur-the-waterfall-with-a-slow-shutterspeed kind of level.

2) Many of the ads are from vendors with bad reputations. I believe they make some sort of claim about requiring a certain level of honesty from anyone they sell ad space from, but it sure doesn't look like they have ever kicked anyone out of the magazine to me.

So what do you have when you have a magazine full of uncritical reviews, the occasional beginnerish article about technique, and a lot ads from stores of dubious virtue? At best a 2 star magazine.

title: Railfan vs. the competition
text: Is literary quality something that should be expected in an enthusiasts' publication?  If so, "Railfan & Railroad" doesn't measure up to the competing publication from Kalmbach.  Or maybe I'm being unfair --  the writing and editing of neither "Railfan" nor "Trains" stands up well to the traditions of a generation ago, when the former was still guided by the late Hal Carstens, and the latter had not begun its (apparently) intentional descent into being a trade publication for the railroad industry, like "Railway Age". Maybe "Trains" had the literary edge in the Good Old Days. "Railfan" seemed the more amateurish, giving a place and voice to unrefined authors who just wanted to share their avocational excitement with like minds.  It should be noted that "Railfan" has emphasized, admirably, the photographic and videographic elements of the hobby since the editorship of Jim Boyd, which still appeals to this reviewer.  Yet neither magazine is the good read that it used to be, leaving me a bit unsatisfied, subscribing just to keep up with developments and current events in my hobby, and choosing this one because I dislike the commercial influence in the competition.

The comments, essays and book reviews in this bimonthly publication are always well researched, written and presented in a straightforward fashion. Certainly, the editorial staff of this outstanding publication is dedicated to the highest standards of excellence as well making sure that Foreign Affairs represents provocative worldwide cutting edge schools of thought.

Korea, Afghanistan, Iraq, Russia, France, Mexico or Colombia...you name it, Foreign Affairs examines it in great detail. To this end, there is no hot spot in global affairs that does not considerable academic or journalistic attention. Foreign Affairs will also focus on sensitive issues such as French Anti-Americanism or Bush's Nuclear Follies with clear and concise observations. One of my favorite magazines and has been for a good 5-6 years. I made the mistake several years ago of subscribing directly through the magazine's website thinking I might qualify somehow (I was obviously delusional) for some of the subscribers' benefits but then I discovered that with the then current exchange rate my AMEX card was charged about $160 for a one year subscription. Ouch. That was the end of my subscription and since I live in NYC I've been buying every month's issue at a local newsstand for $10. If you don't have that option where you live, the cost of the Amazon subscription is just a little bit more than I'm paying per issue which isn't terrible, all things being relative, of course.

I look forward to it every month and often wait to purchase it late in the week so I can look at it over a glass of wine, or two, during the weekend because I like to take my time and enjoy it. Like any magazine, some months are better than others but every issue seems to have a gem or two and I incorporated several ideas I'd seen in the magazine in my recent apartment renovation with great results. All in all, highly recommended for someone with modern tastes and maybe a bit of wander lust thrown in for good measure.

title: Best source of information, if that's all you have.
text:
My nephew was sentenced to 24 years in the "Ham" for a stupid stunt when he was 17 (attempted robbery with two 16 year old boys). The "Ham" is an old state prison near Lovelady, Texas. Clyde, from Bonnie and Clyde, served time there. There are no TVs, little access to outside information, no air conditioning or heating, and certainly no cell phones.

Families are not allowed to send gifts. The only option families have is to pay a publisher to send books and magazines. Even these are reviewed by the prison officials for "acceptable" content. You can't send holiday gifts, nothing but letters, books and magazines. I received an official letter from a prison official saying "you can't send extra stamps in your letters.. it's a 'violation'".

Well my nephew loves USA Today! It's the best source of news and cultural information that's printed daily, and it's a great holiday gift. His release date is not for another 4 years, but since rehabilitation is mostly "virtual" in Texas, USA Today is helping to prepare him for the shock he'll have when he steps outside that prison after 24 years. Without USA Today he wouldn't know much about cell phones, personal computers, gps devices, etc. Now when we visit him, we can talk politics, technology and national events with him. Without USA Today our conversations revolve around prison food with is pretty bad.

For industry Proffesionals, Wanna be's, Campaign observers,Political Scientists,Students and personally I think Reporter's would do well to look in it's pages. This magazine comes stuffed full of current strategies, reviews of new voter mapping software as well as articles written by campaign staff who compare their experiences on different campaigns and share some of the late night jokes. There is voter trend information that will fascinate any demographer and advise on how to put together a campaign strategy.Rather than linger over poll results, this magazine is more likely to describe the larger polling organizations,their techniques and who they are aligned with. Of particular value are the short blurbs in which strategists will debate on which type of polls, if any, to spend your limited campaign dollars.
.Campaigns & Elections comes just infrequently enough that you don't feel bogged down during your insanely busy time. Fascinating analysis in the post national election issue which broke down successful voter blocks and mobilization techniques. A special issue each year is dedicated to a listing of Campaign Consultants which reads a bit like walking through a bazaar.

title: These ppl r scum
text:
Sorry that was crass but that's how I feel. I am totally livid at this so-called magazine and it's vulturous practices. My daughter's baby died in utero. She had only found out she was pregnant a few weeks before so thankfully she came out of it all right. A month or so goes by and we start getting this packet from American Baby magazine. I hated to bring this up to my daughter but I had to find out if she sent away for anything or something, so we racked our brains to try and find out how this happened because it seemed a little too random to be coincidence and we couldn't come up with anything. She said the only thing she bought baby related were pregnancy tests at Walgreen's and she paid for it in cash. We thought it was possibly some strange fluke and left it at that. Another month goes by and now we're getting the magazine. This is too much! I hunted around for the phone number and talked to one of their operators, the rudest person I think I've ever talked to and they said they'd take our names off the list. When I asked how we got ON their list they said she must have purchased something recently that was associated with babies and she was put on their mailing list from a prior purchase. That would actually make sense if she actually had purchased anything like that. She swears up and down she didn't purchase anything other than the preg. tests and I believe her. Even if she wanted to, she didn't have the means at the time to purchase anything else. If I could give this company a negative number I would, I would give them a negative 20. There's nothing good about them - just all kinds of wrong.

Oh and to show where their heads and hearts (if you want to call it that) are at, here's a sample of my phone call:

---"I'm upset that my daughter is getting these unsolicited magazines and offers now especially because she lost the baby."

---"Okay, I've taken you off the list. Is there anything else I can help you with?"

---"No."

---"Okay, have a nice day."

Just as curt as you can possibly please. You know, a person with a heart might have at least pretended that they gave a damn and actually said they were sorry for our loss and for the intrusion. He didn't even make a show of it. Rotten, this company's just rotten to the core.

title: A German classic - see the Ducks and Mickey as never before!
text:
This is the monthly publication of European Disney stories, centering on the Ducks and Mickey Mouse, and it's a treat from heaven. I grew up reading these books - they're about the size of a medium-thick paperback. This venerable publication celebrates its 50th anniversary this year, and shows no signs of stopping. In fact there are special editions of this book, but as far as I know those aren't available for subscription outside of Germany.
A few points to the characters: these are NOT the American versions of Donald and Mickey, they are the European ones. This is not Carl Barks stuff! Most stories are by Italian artists, some by Spanish and Dutch artists, and oh my yes, those guys know how to write and draw a fine story! Get ready for a permanently broke Donald who is lazy and at odds with the world in general and his family in particular. The family dynamics of the Ducks are quite adversary, although the storylines are mellower now. Scrooge is only too happy to take advantage of his relatives (and anyone else, for that matter), his stinginess and avarice are pathological.
US readers will be surprised to encounter Donald's superhero alter ego Phantomias, who has protected Duckburg since the early 70's. Other rather unfamiliar characters include Kater Karlo (Pegleg Pete), Indiana Goof, Inspector Issel (Mr Casey) and Gundel Gaukeley (Magica DeSpell).
The stories can be read without worrying about previous editions, unless a story is a continuation of an older one, in which case references are made as necessary. Continuity isn't an issue here, and considering there's almost 500 editions, that's a good thing! The books are being reprinted, but older issues are not available by subscription, and the publisher doesn't ship outside of Europa.

It goes without saying that the writing is in German, and it's current to the newest slang, which often happens to be an English word.

I love these books, and I was more than happy to subscribe!

Because the writing is very sloppy; it appears the editor/publisher never actually reads what he publishes. The articles are incoherently written, full of typos and, on those rare occasions when the writer is actually communicating, frequently factually wrong. I've written the editor/publisher several times asking him to make corrections of fact, but he never does. Finally, I wrote asking that he cancel my subscription and refund the balance of my money -- but no reply there, either. Indeed, it looks to me like the editor/publisher writes his own Letters to the Editor section, as the letters are always flattering -- and completely content-free. It's too bad this magazine has existed for 25 years, thus likely discouraging anyone else from taking a stab at publishing for the beginning consumer video market. There is definitely a need for good writing published on a regular basis for that audience -- but Videomaker is not that publication.

title: Best Mag for PC Enthusiasts
text:
I've been reading this magazine for about 2 years (front-to-back) and it is absolutely the best pc magazine out there. The reviews are so well done that I often refer to old issues; something I can't say about competing magazines.
The articles are useful and succinct, usually covering issues well ahead of other publications. It is well organized and allows you to glance through it with their summarizing "Verdict" boxes on each review. The editors are very good about keeping with their readers, effectively relating to them.
A flagship occurance, as many other readers will tell you, that sets this magazine apart is that you might find a review telling you how horrible the product is on one page and on the next see an advertisement for that same product. I build many computers and I rarely disagree with their reviews. Another useful item is the benchmark, which lets you compare system and laptop performance to others they have reviewed as well as to your own.
For hardcore users, the magazine provides dependable, in-depth reviews. For beginners, it might be very intimidating, but after a couple issues, you should catch on to the style and humor enough to know more than the average person.
A con not mentioned in other reviews is that their web-site isn't all that spectacular. However, they finally hired someone to work on it, so it should improve.

title: Tarnish On the Fine Reputation of Natl Geographic
text:
This isn't your old-school National Geographic. When I was growing up, my siblings and I used our vast collection of Natl Geographics--going back to the 1950s--to research school projects. I have always thought of the organization that produced the magazine as a national educational treasure, but their kids' magazine calls their reputation into question.

My mother-in-law sent a Natl Geo Kids subscription as a gift for my two daughters. I was excited for them to start receiving it. Now I throw it away before they see it. As other reviewers have reported, the ads are for media products and junk food, and they are often incorporated into sponsored content sections. Aesthetically and content-wise, it doesn't give kids a lot of credit--it's In Your Face with garish colors and marketing-type copy.

I have written email to the editors of both the kids and adult versions of National Geographic saying I ditched my adult subscription offer in protest. As long as this terrible kids' magazine exists, it tars the reputation of National Geographic Magazine. They should send my kids an apology and a free subscription to the real Natl Geographic. It is, in this reviewer's opinion, an essential monthly read for every aficionado of the mainland European railway scene.

title: The New Yorker of the Fantasy/SciFi Genre
text: What sets F&SF Mag apart from the other digest-sized magazines that deliver speculative fiction is that F&SF chooses, almost every month, to transcend the genres it represents instead of remaining within the definitions and boxes that limit the other magazines.  There don't seem to be any hard and fast rules concerning the stories that appear in this magazine except that they be really well written, and compellingly readable.  The stories run all over the fertile woodland of Fantasy and Science Fiction and every month hold many surprises.  There really hasn't been a magazine this satisfying since the old Twilight Zone magazine.  In the end, it isn't about hard science or speculation about what might happen (in a scientific way).  This is a magazine about stories for people who love to read them.

title: Thorough Descriptions of Growers, Winemakers and Wines
text:
After reading a neighbor's Wine Advocate while catsitting, I decided to subscribe (to the electronic version eRobertParker). What I like about the reviews is actually not the numerical ratings, or even Parker's adjectives, but his incredibly detailed notes on the grape blends involved, vineyards, producers and winemaking. For example, here's a review of one of my favorite wines taken from the April 2004 Wine Advocate, which is fairly typical of a Parker review:

2001 Numanthia

Numanthia

Toro, Spain

Tempranillo (a dry red table wine)

The flagship offering, the 2001 Numanthia, is fashioned from a 70-100 year old Tinta de Toro vineyard planted at a 2300 foot elevation. After a 28 day maceration, the wine undergoes malolactic in barrel, is aged 19 months in new French oak, and is bottled without fining or filtration. The spectacular, opaque purple-colored 2001 offers an explosive nose of melted licorice, barbecue smoke, blackberries, creme de cassis, camphor, and graphite. Full-bodied with gorgeously rich, concentrated fruit, a layered texture, and tremendous purity, it can be drunk young, but should hit its prime in 1-2 years, and last for 10-15.

Wine Advocate includes info on U.S. importers, a rating, and an often unreliable estimated cost (especially "bargains" which tend to be affected by Parker's ratings). All in all, a set of information that's not available elsewhere, typically not even from a winemaker's web site, when there is one.

Parker is not the only taster. There's also Pierre Rovani and Daniel Thomases, who carve up the world by region. Parker seems to have dibs on my favorite regions: Chateauneuf and Hermitage in the Rhone, Toro and Ribera del Duero in Spain, and California Zinfandel. On the downside, the coverage of regions is uneven, which is forgivable given the size of the winemaking world. I, for one, would like to see more Alsatian whites reviewed.

The Wine Advocate reviews not only wines, but whole regions. They note not only who's doing what in a region, but what the weather was like for a given year and what the growers and winemakers did given the conditions. The overall ratings for regions and vintages have proven very reliable in my experience.

I prefer the web site to the magazine, because it has all the back issues, and allows you to search. It also includes wine news, amateurish (though funny) cartoons, and lifestyle pieces filed under "Hedonist's Gazette", where you can read about dinners and tastings that would cost us punters thousands of dollars if they could be bought at all.

title: Interweave Group BAIT & SWITCH
text:
Over the past four to five years, I have spent several hundred dollars in publications, video downloads, eMags, etc. pertaining to my craft of the moment. I picked up spinning in the past two years and taught myself how to spin from Interweave's vast online resources. All in all, I am now able to spin with very good consistency, 3 ply sock yarn or 3 ply lace, on up to worsted weight using several drafting methods. I also am adept at plying, carding, combing and dying wool, alpaca, and cotton. All this from the information I obtained from Interweave and the virtual Judith Mackenzie, who has been at my side whether she knows it or not. I will not give Interweave a higher score because of an issue that I ran into this morning, which has happened several times before: Bait and switch price marketing.

Numerous time I have found coupon codes that will give a discount during the checkout process only to mysteriously disappear before the bill in finalized. I've been offered $1 off on third party issues of Colorways eMags, through iTunes, only to be charged the full price by iTunes. And once again this morning I received a VIP Early Pass to receive 70% overstock items before everyone else since I am 'such a good customer.' The item is advertised in the email at $8.98. It shows up in the shopping cart as $20.98 even after I log into my account and go to PayPal. And I've been down the road of completing the purchase and it 'supposedly' sorts itself out in the end. It does not. You have to call to sort it out if you want you discount. Even then, they make it sound as if I have done something wrong. I warned customer service the last time that this happened that I would write a scathing review it it happened again, so here it is.

Cheating is stealing and I don't appreciate it. I challenge Interweave to fix this problem and make it right.

title: COVERS EUROPEAN OPERA SINGERS AND PRODUCTIONS
text:
Over the years I have mostly browsed this magazine at Tower Records, buying an occasional issue to study in detail. The demise of Tower ended this. As someone who has to look up every other German word, I can only give a general impression of it's content.

Before opera on VHS and then DVD, Opernglas was a way to study regietheater productions. By looking at the photos and translating only the photo captions I was able to get an impression of regietheater early on. Recently I have used auto-translate to get an idea of what is being covered. Of course auto-translate is not context sensitive, ie it does only half the job. Making sense out of some music articles in English can be hard enough, let alone reading the same material in German. I know people with far more language skills who don't follow German opera news stories, because it takes more time than is available to them.

Unlike Opera News which is mostly about the Met, Opernglas covers many opera companies, some of which are very small. Coverage is not limited to Germany. I cannot say this with certainty, but coverage seems to be even handed.

Opernglas is very good at covering emerging European singers long before they become known in the USA.

If you only want an occasional article, you can download them for about 3.50 Euro each. Unless you know the title, year and issue and enter that into Opernglas' search accurately, you will not find it. In other words there is no way to search for an artist name to see if there are any articles on that artist, unless you already have the year and month. Try running a search for 5 years, ie sixty issues, to find what you are looking for, not fun. Of course this is a good way to keep the print version viable.

Conclusion: This is a magazine that I would buy if I was going to do long term studies of the European opera scene. It would be nice if someone who reads it on a regular basis would give us a review. Low interest in this magazine in America is, in my considered opinion, a reflection on us, not the magazine.

title: Beware Vanity Fair Subscription Renewal SCAM
text:
I enjoyed Vanity Fair magazine for several years but I chose to not renew it in January 2005. They sent the usual renewal notices and I tossed them out, and the magazine stopped coming.

Now in July 2005 I got a harassing letter from "National Credit Audit Corporation" threatening me if I don't pay the $15 account. I did not renew this and I don't owe it, but the tone of the letter is serious.

With some research on the Net I see that Vanity Fair is using an unreputable firm to harass people into renewing.

Anyhow this is finally getting picked up by the mainstream media such as the San Francisco Chronicle, which reported that VF's sister publication, WIRED Magazine, is doing the same thing (they are both Conde Naste publications).

NOTE this is NOT related to Amazon.com, and I am not saying if you subscribe via Amazon that this will happen. It seems to be part of a certain low-rate offer that contained certain language about "auto-renewal" that nobody could possibly read, it's so small. I am writing a letter to the magazine, the credit agency, and the attorneys general of New York and Florida.

The magazine is great, the journalism is top rate. But just try to stop your subscription, you might face the same dunning.

text: Reason cannot be labeled conservative or leftist.  Nor is it an extremist libertarian magazine like Liberty, fawning over Ayn Rand.  It bases its commentary on the assumption that, if we have some faith, our chaotic culture will lead somewhere good.  But if we try to monitor and control it excessively, we will dampen human creativity and end up muddled and conflicted.  Reason takes on all aspects of culture and assumes an international perspective.  Its arguments are laid out carefully but contain a percolating sense of indignation at our increasingly repressive environment.  At the same time, they are more informative than polemical; each report is grounded in specifics - quotes, anecdotes, studies. title: Amazon subscriptions -- don't waste your time
text:
I ordered this on 4/9 and waited patiently the 6-10 weeks they say it takes for it to arrive.
After the estimated time passed I called the subscription service and I was told they would fix the problem, contact me when they had fixed it and make sure I received a full year of the magazine. The nexy day I had not heard back so I called again and was told that the first person I spoke to entered nothing in the system. The second phone call I made was actually entered in the system and again I was told someone would contact me to verify. No one called me so I called a third time.
The third time I call I find out that the magazine is now estimated for delivery in September (5 months after my original order date). Super. So I decide to cancel.
Initially they want to "calculate the number of issues" I have received and deduct that from my total - even though the reason I am cancelling is because I have received nothing. Great.
Finally they agree to refund my money in full. Here's the best part: since I paid with a gift card, they will mail me a check! That can take 4-6 weeks.
So, in short, I have no magazine and no money to show for it. Had I sent in a subscription card directly I would have spent a few dollars more but given that time is money and I have spent a great deal of time dealing with the customer service at Amazon I think I would have broken even.
Lesson learned.
Never buying magazines from Amazon.

The reasons I enjoyed these magazines: They discuss hair, make-up, guys, etc. But they put a Christian spin on these things. People think that because we are Christians that we don't have the same interest. Well, I am here to tell you that Christian girls do like guys. Also, in their teenage years and now even earlier, they are concerned with hair and make-up. So if the magazine gives tips on how to apply make-up that's great.

In addition, this magazine usually introduces a peer (usually a famous young actress) that is a Christian. These are the role models I want for my children. Not actress/actors that have drinking and drug problems. The stories are inspiring and Christian based.

The section of brio that allows kids to ask questions, also opens doors for girls to find answers to questions they never new and maybe even never thought to ask. It also allows for discussion of embarrassing moments and how to handle issues with friends, such as a friend that is experiementing with drugs or something. I see nothing wrong with that. And I think that the responses are great for kids to understand what type of situation needs addressing...such as when should I tell my Mom about this friend?

title: Slightly inconsistent magazine with several great reads a year
text:
I've been reading Esquire for close to two decades now. During that time I've started and stopped several other magazine subscriptions, but Esquire has always kept coming in my mailbox. I'll be honest, it's not the best or most consistent magazine out there. So, why do I keep subscribing?

The good:

1. Every few months, Esquire has some great journalism articles geared towards laypersons. I currently get the Economist, and while I love that magazine, it's not accessible to most (price, topics, writing style).
2. What I've Learned -- It's by far my favorite section in the magazine and contains 1 page of anecdotes/lessons from living legends (and up & coming stars) in sports, politics, acting, writing, etc. Esquire should really considering binding all of these into a stand alone book.
3. The fashion advice column (while still aimed at a wealthier demographic) is a lot more accessible than that in other men's magazines.
4. A couple times a year, there is some great short fiction.

The bad:

1. In the last few years, the pages have been bloating with more ads, but it's nowhere near as bad as GQ or many others.
2. With the success of magazines like Maxim, Esquire has unfortunately begun including similar humor and columns aimed at a younger audience. I wish they'd go back to their roots.
3. In recent years, the magazine has certainly begun leaning left, and it shows in nearly every issue. It seems to me in the 90s, the magazine did a great job of remaining impartial -- or maybe it's just something I'm finally noticing as I age.

In short, for how cheap the magazine is, it's a steal to get several great reads a year.

text:
The first rule I learned in Journalism 101 (shortly before dropping the class) was "Always remain objective". At OXM, editors and writers alike check thier objectivity at the door.
OXM is a nicely laid out magazine. Unfortunatley it's content is very weak. When I read a video game magazine I want it to first be informative. While OXM is "informative", it's the XBox "attitude" that gets in the way. The editorial and writing staff try so hard to be hip, cool and edgey that they come across as a joke. If you read in between the pot shots taken at Sony and the PS2 there is some relevant information. But it tends to get lost amidst the puns and attempts at being humorous.
The second thing I want from a magazine, are objective opinions. With OXM, objectivity goes out the window. Though most games that are reviewed are pretty informative, often times a mediocre game will score significantly higher than in other game magazines. Which makes me wonder exactly who is writing these reviews. Also, every issue is loaded with countless digs at Sony and Nintendo. After the first few pages it becomes childish and unamusing.
The saving grace of the magazine is the demo disc. On it you can get some downloads including bonus levels for some games. Unfortunatley it's not included here.
Considering the content of this magazine, I'd recomend picking it up on an issue by issue basis depending on what is included in the demo disc. For a better all around objectively written game magazine, I'd recomend Game Informer.

this issue (roughly):
90 pages total=
13 pages of projects (generous estimate, most are part of a page)
13 pages of gift/ shopping ideas (not including ads)
18 pages food/ recipes
28 full page ads

This is a magazine that anyone who loves to tinker will absolutely love.

title: Beware BHG aggressive collections!
text:
My wife got one of those calls soliciting magazines that mentioned BHG. Since we were moving in the near future she refused. A short time later Better Homes and Gardens started coming to the house. We didn't order the magazine and couldn't figure how to cancel. Subsequently we moved but we got a bill from BHG stating we will be TAKEN TO COLLECTIONS over this bogus subscription. I just did some internet searches and found that BHG has been using this tactic for many years. I found an article on poynter.org from 2011 that reports that "Better Homes and Gardens promises to end threatening renewal letters". Three years later they are still doing it. We figure an overzealous sales person signed her up so they can get their commission.
I went to their web site to try to contact them and you can't unless you have your magazine info - but guess what? They put the magazines in an clear wrapper so you usually toss that info when you open the magazine.
If you get anything from BHG that you didn't order do make sure to put a stop to it as soon as you can. I'm surprised that they continue to do this seven years after they said they wouldn't.

title: The New Yorker of Science Magazines
text:
Giving this magazine such a lofty epithet may seem a bit presumptuous, but for a non scientifically trained outsider this magazine offers a fresh and challenging look at the fast paced world of science that doesn't shy away from humor and the use of terms and ideas that may require its readers to go online and define a term. And in some cases it may inspire the reader to pick up a book on science by such greats as Hawking and Greene in order to better grasp some of the concepts dealing with time, space and atoms. This magazine isn't dumbed down. It includes well placed and efficient illustrations to help explain some of the more abstract points. It is not designed in the way popular magazinea are, in so much as they only touch upon a topic in the simplest manner and then move on before the audience is lost. Yet this magazine keeps the attention of the reader by combining explanatory notes that help people with no background knowledge have some grasp of the topic and by using humor and well written articles to clearly make their points.
For a magazine with a serious and well researched list of topics having small cartoons the likes of the New Yorker shows how comfortable this magazine is with itself. From the moment I picked up this magazine for the first time I felt like every word I read mattered and was worth my time to read. (Not true of many other magazines) American Scientist may not have the audience of Discover or National Geographic, nor is it as accessible as said titles, but for those with a true interest in science willing to challenge themselves and commit to real learning this magazine may be a perfect fit. At $4.95 it is certainly worth it to pick a copy on the news stand and try it out.

text: Generations of my family have subscribed to this magazine.  I lost track of it for a while and recently resubscribed.  It is a great magazine.  It is full of the human interest stories, and "good news" articles that we all wish there were more of.  Regular news is sensationalist, violence, and politics.  Bad news.  This magazine is the good stuff--an article about a military service dog who finds a good adoptive home after his retirement and the struggles that entails, one on how laughter is scientifically good for you, a Good Samaritan article on a guy climbing into a burning car to rescue a terrified, injured driver.  All of this interspersed with true short stories (a paragraph long) of goofy stuff that happens in real life that is just plain funny. title: A New Competitor for 'The Gramophone'
text:
This glossy British classical music magazine that focuses primarily on recordings was founded in 2000 by, I believe, some disgruntled former 'Gramophone' writers. The staff of writers include such well-known reviewers as Martin Anderson, Hugh Canning, Jed Distler, Mortimer H. Frank, Harris Goldsmith, Julian Haylock, Simon Heighes, Robert Layton, Donald Manildi, Andrew Porter, Charles Timbrell, Raymond S. Tuttle, John Warrack and others. As you can see, the writers primarily come from England but there are far more American reviewers than write for 'Gramophone,' giving it a bit more trans-Atlantic balance than the older magazine. It is, as they say, 'for those who know their music but who are prepared to be further enlightened, appreciate good sound-reproduction, without the need for gimmicks and who want up-to-date, authoritative comment on the vast number of new and historical classical recordings being released worldwide.' There are monthly review sections for orchestral, chamber, instrumental, choral, vocal and opera CDs as well as for DVDs and books. Issues also contain

- A frank, topical and pertinent editorial

- An extensive and detailed Index to the reviews

- Letters to the Editor

- A list of new international releases

- News pages and obituaries

- Special extensive features on major repertoire (with exhaustive comparisons of extant recordings)

- A Directory of record company websites

There are no sections dealing with sound reproduction or new electronic gadgets. One plus is that there is a good deal of attention paid to historical recordings. For instance, in a recent issue there was an extensive section about historical opera re-issues.

The writing is generally both graceful and informed. It is rare that I don't learn a good deal from an issue, and I tend to read every word of every article. The only drawback for American subscribers (and the reason I've awarded only 4 stars) is that, with the currently disadvantageous exchange rate for the US dollar against the British pound, it is a bit expensive. I, however, would not like to be without it.

I hope this description helps prospective subscribers decide whether this is their cup of tea.

Scott Morrison

title: Kelvins? List a more familiar scale next to it for the novice sky gazer.
text:
The magazine is chock full of fantastic photographs and drawings.
Yes, it competes with Sky and Telescope.
I will give it five stars. If I could I would give it 4.9 stars.
Here is the reason and my only beef at this time.
I have been reading both magazines for decades,
since they were printed in black and white.
I am a semi retired professor of astronomy. I have
been teaching astronomy at all grade levels, elementary,
through the high school grades and at the university level, AST.101
if I may.
My complaint is that the magazine authors list the temperature of
objects, like the surface ( as far as a surface can be detected )
of Jupiter in Kelvins. What? Kelvins. Not centigrade, Celsius or even
Fahrenheit, (oh my gosh, how dare I mention the Fahrenheit scale
when that is the scale that the weather people use in telling us the
temperature here in the United States.)
Yes, on the internet the Kelvin scale is said to be used supposedly by the
scientific community. Funny thing though, not too many
scientists use Kelvin. When I watch the P.B.S. and take in a great
documentary program the scientists ALWAYS use the
centigrade scale. By the way, Celsius and centigrade are the same.
My take on this is that Astronomy magazine is doing a disservice
to many new astronomers and people of all ages by using the
Kelvin scale.
Try going on the internet and finding a conversion scale to
convert Kelvins to Fahrenheit. It is impossible. One needs a
degree in advanced mathematics to accomplish this.
I hate to say it, but I believe by using the Kelvin scale instead
of a more normal and useable scale the authors are trying to
be stuffy and arrogant.
It is like in education, from where my background is. The
educational community uses phrases and terms that are
foreign to the normal parent.
Come on Astronomy and Sky and Telescope, if you insist
on using a Kelvin number, then right next to it, use a
centigrade or Fahrenheit number so the teen ager or novice
is not scared away from this beautiful hobby. We want to encourage
new star gazers, not scare them away or frustrate them.
Respectfully,
Jim Cook

title: Forbes delivers high quality articles, but its liberal bashing gets tiring
text:
Forbes is a conservative business publication that delivers excellent reporting and feature articles. The content is concise, blunt, and to the point because Forbes recognizes the importance of time and clarity. The magazine is especially strong in providing advice to individuals, and businesses about upcoming changes in the tax code, and legislation that would impact the bottom line. However, I have found that the editorial content has become a venue for editors to make personal attacks towards Obama and the democratic party.

Pros:
As a business magazine, Forbes does an excellent job at delivering succinct articles about business, economics, and stocks. In each issue, the magazine devotes a large section towards dispensing advice about money and investing. There is a depth and detail that can only be found in this magazine. Forbes assumes its readers are astute and smart, and is unwilling to dumb down its content to boost circulation numbers. In a recent article, Forbes provided detailed advice about retirement accounts, and their tax implications.

Cons:
Forbes can improve its publication by editorializing less and focus more on business issues, and less bashing upon liberal politics. For example, Forbes can take the lead and recommend to businesses ways to reduce health care costs by writing about Safeway, which has been able to tame healthcare inflation. If the magazine authors wants to express their political beliefs, then they are working for the wrong magazine.

title: Wonderful reporting and feature articles from around the world
text:
In an era of declining journalism, National Geographic shines above all else as a benchmark for quality, and photojournalism. They have recently won multiple ellie's the equivalent of the Pulizer prize in the magazine industry.

Each issue includes one or two features articles from around the world. While the magazine contains advertisements, they have placed ads in the front and back of the magazine so that feature articles are not interrupted by an annoying gaudy ad, a practice often seen in other magazines. The quality of the photos are simply amazing; the magazine uses a high quality paper to print quality photos not seen in any other magazine out there.

It is not fair that other reviewers, provide a lower rating for this magazine because it can be found cheaper elsewhere. National Geographic provides a lower introductory rate. However, once you get past the first year, subscribers need to pay the default rate of $34.

title: The slow decline of a great magazine
text:
I started reading The Atlantic in 2004. Back then The Atlantic provided insightful and interesting articles covering Iraq and Afghanistan, and occasionally included some fiction.

In the last five years, I have witnessed a slight decline in the quality of this magazine. No doubt this is due to the decline in advertising revenues of this magazine. The Atlantic has scaled down and axed the fiction section from its monthly publication. Fiction is now published annually. Recent covers have included tacky and cheesy headlines designed to capture attention and are more appropriate for a tabloid than The Atlantic. Examples have included

- The Britney Show
- The Passion of Alec Baldwin
- If Kim Jong Il Used Facebook

Despite it's recent shortcomings, I would recommend the Atlantic to anyone interested in reading about global affairs, finance, culture, and politics.

title: Rolling Stone decent for the mainstream audience.

***

It is a little quirky but it is an excellent magazine to discover good films, and music. There is a reason why Wall Street Journal called Paste the 'Best American Music Magazine.'

title: Useless after November 2014 magazine redesign
text:
Consumer Reports got a new President and Editor in November 2014. The magazine's format and content has taken a drastic change for the worse.
It appears they hired a reject graphic designer from WIRED magazine. (That's not a compliment.)

One can't tell the new reviews from the rehashed data presented in a previous issue.
Of the items reviewed, only the top 25% are listed. So the reader is left to wonder if the vacuum at Sears is a loser or just a model that wasn't reviewed.
They got rid of the product photos. For example, the review of vacuum cleaners contained no images of vacuum cleaners.
Heavy emphasis on health care in environmental issues at the expense of product reviews.
Graphics are overly busy, messy.
Public Opinion is presented as if it's newsworthy or actionable.
Car Reviews are now down to one paragraph. Discussion of a car's highlights and lowlights are gone. Only highlight is CR's independent mpg measurement. Vehicles that use premium gas are no longer identified.

As another review said, there are tidbits here and there, but it's a entertainment magazine now.

It is disappointing to see a misguided President and Editor value style over substance and ruin an institution like Consumer Reports.

title: Buyer Beware, term not as advertised
text:
Amazon advertises this as 1 year or 3 month subscriptions, but Bloomberg does not count them by time. Bloomberg counts your subscription by issues sent. One year by Amazon is 50 issues at Bloomberg. In the past year Bloomberg counted 7 of its issues as double issues, so 50 issues was 43 weeks. In other words, if you ordered a one-year subscription on Amazon, Bloomberg finished that in less than 11 full months. To check this out for yourself, your Amazon Magazine Subscription Manager will give one date, based on Amazon's calendar thinking, and your account on Bloomberg will give a rather different date based on number of issues sent.

Great magazine, but beware the difference in Amazon's and Bloomberg's subscription accounting

text:
Entertainment Weekly is a magazine about Movies, Tv shows, Books, Music and the celebrities involved in such.

I will discuss the sections of the magazine then my impressions.

"The Must List" lists the top 10 things we love this week from any category

"First Look" section talks about new projects coming out of hollywood

"News and Notes" involves news anywthing from why shows are cancelled to new judges on "Idol"

"Monitor" involves Births, Marriages, Arrests, Deaths and such.

"Exclusives" is where EW gets the first information on ground breaking movies/shows

"Movies" Rated & Reviewed
"Tv Shows" Rated & Reviewed
"TV What to Watch" A Tv guide like section for the week
"Music" Rated & Reviewed
"Books" Rated & Reviewed

My feelings on this magazine is that it is infromative, but I feel that most of thier rating and reviews for books/movies/tv is based more on how artistic the reviewer sees them rather than how enjoyable they are to watch or read. And the book section talks mostly about Nonfiction & Memoirs. They rarely go near fiction in their rating & reviews.

Together these things make me think this magazine targets an older more refined audience than me.

Still I will probably continue to subscribe to this magazine as it helps me be mindful of setting my DVR for new upcoming shows. And also what to add to my Netflix Queue.

(NOTE: I prefer and highly recommend the Bi-monthly "Sci fi Magazine" it covers scifi,fantasy,horror in TV, Movies and Books. It is very much like Entertainment weekly, but delivered every other month and is much thicker. It is my favorite magazine for entertainment)

text:
The magazine is great (most of the numbers) however their subscription process is the worst.
First of all, this subscription here says that you will get 12 numbers. When you order here, it took 2 months before you get the first number. But what I did not know is that these two months are calculated in the order time, so instead of having 12 numbers in the order you will get only the numbers that come when the magazine starts coming. For example, if you order in February and your order processing takes 2 months, your first number is in April... you would think that you will get your last number then the next year in March (12 numbers, right?), wrong: your order ends January because you actually ordered in February even if you did not get February and March numbers....

I am not going to order this magazine again.

title: BAD BAD BAD Customer Service IF Any
text:
For Christmas I went to the "O"'s website to order a subscription for my sister. The subscription site is not very clear (Though to my own error - I tend to be quick with the fingers - as my husband calls me Mrs Clicky-Clicky). I finally saw where at the very bottom in very fine writing it says "gift subscription". Once I finally got to the page, I believe I misread or clicked to fast and accidently selected a "treat yourself to a subscription". Needless to say, by the time I realized it, it was too late.

I searched all over the site, back and forth, re-Googling, everything, but there is not one single 1-800 # for any type of customer service to be found. I ended up having to go through 5 screens to get to a customer service function for my situation. The best I could come up with was 'Cancel subscription'. But the site also previously said to wait 6-9 weeks for processing before canceling, if any magazines were shipped you would be refunded the difference.

Since I did not want this magazine at all, I wrote the customer service anyway. Once I typed in my explanation, etc and hit "Send" it wouldn't send. Even refreshing kept my information on the screen. After clicking send 10x - it finally went through.

2 days later I noticed the charged for the subscription on my credit card 2x. The next day I got an email response from their customer service stating "We do not show a subscription for yourself, your gift subscription will be entered into our files and begin with Dec 2006 issue. You will receive an invoice in the near future, and upon receipt of your

payment of $18.00 your gift subscription(s) will continue for the full

number of issues ordered."... AN INVOICE???? To continue? They already charged my credit card Twice?!

I emailed back. It's been 7 days and no response to my email. So I went back to the website to try from their customer service page again, and it won't go at all, no matter how many times I select send.

I'm out $36 (though to my error) but have no way to be able to resolve this issue due to the lack of either a customer service willing to do things thoroughly the first time (i.e their 1 response to me) or a customer service dept that is obtainable or reachable.

BEWARE BEWARE BEWARE BEWARE BEWARE

title: BEWARE!  Fraudulent invoicing tactics.  Do not buy!!!
text: As much as I enjoy reading the Oprah magazine, I will NEVER again purchase an annual subscription.  This magazine (or their publishing company) is downright shameful in the ways in which they harass their customers.  Immediately after I ordered AND PAID FOR my annual subscription, I began receiving notices from the "invoicing bureau" at O, The Oprah Magazine claiming that I owed money for my subscription.  But I had already paid for the year IN FULL, and the FUTURE expiration date of my subscription was clearly printed on the invoice (indicating that my subscription was active for another 8 months).  There is NO PHONE NUMBER printed on these invoices, so I had to search online for a customer service phone number (finally found the number in a review on Amazon.com - it's 888-446-4438 by the way).  When I contacted the customer service department, the lady explained that I wasn't exactly receiving "a bill;" they were simply marketing the opportunity to purchase a future subscription.  What a joke! They could've fooled me!  The "marketing piece" stated that I would be in default if I didn't promptly pay the amount due.  The "marketing piece" made me think I was about to be reported to a collection agency.  HOW SHAMEFUL!  I wonder how many people fall for this deceptive marketing scheme and pay for a future subscription just because they're afraid they're in trouble?  Oprah Winfrey should be ashamed that her name is associated with such a scam.  BEWARE!!!  Do not buy a subscription to O, The Oprah Magazine.  I promise you will regret it almost immediately!

title: Oprah: The Magazine
text: Purchasing the subscription to the Oprah Magazine is one of the best investments I've made.  I used to buy it every now and then on the newstand for the inflated newstand price, but now it comes straight to my mailbox for a fraction of the cost, well ahead of the time it hits the newstands.  The articles are always timely and on topics that interest me and which I feel would interest other women---topics to do with body image, money, sex, self-esteem, relationships of all types, assertiveness, giving and receiving and also topics that deal with difficult or traumatic issues like child abuse, cancer, losing a child, etc.  It is not only the topics in and of themselves that are of interest but the focus the writers take when writing about them that make the reading so engrossing. One might find articles on these same topics in other magazines, but the content of the articles in the Oprah Magazine is, in my opinion, far superior. The writing is always excellent and the editing superb.  While I may take the month to finish reading the magazine, I read it cover to cover and some articles have such a great impact on me that I cut them out save them so that I can read them again in the future. The advertisements are, for the most part, an enhancement to the magazine and not an annoying interruption like they are in most magazines.  They are well chosen and focus on products and services that  nurture and pamper. The prices are often on the high side, but what is advertised is generally high quality and fits with one of the main messages of the magazine, "Take good care of yourself".

title: Country Living isn't what it used to be!
text:
I have lived on a farm for the last 23 years and this magazine has nothing to do with real honest-to-goodness country living. I recently accepted an offer for a free trial issue of Country Living. I grew up on a farm and my mom always had an issue of Country Living next to her chair. We savored and saved our favorite issues. They were a visual feast for the eyes with glossy full page photos of the loveliest of country homes and gardens to drool over. When I had kids I quit subscribing because I didn't have time to look at magazines anymore.
I anticipated my first issue of Country Living in many years with these memories in mind. Not only did a bill arrive a month before my first issue, I was confused when it finally did arrive. Surely this wasn't Country Living magazine? I double checked the cover, and it said Country Living but it did not resemble the magazine I remember at all. There were ads, ads, and...more ads!! There were tons of tiny pictures of product lists crammed on almost every page with numbers and arrows pointing to stuff, stuff, and more stuff. title: Late Delivery
text:
I purchased this subscription for my wife as a 2012 Christmas gift because she kept buying them off the rack and paying a lot more. Well, lo and behold, that's what they want you to do because the last 4 issues she has received have been a few weeks after they hit news stands. As of right now, in Mid-March, the April edition is already at the supermarket and she has yet to receive it. She loves the magazine, but it's frustrating because typical magazine subscriptions get mailed to subscribers before they hit stands.

I'm not a consipracy theorist, but I am in finance and looking at Time, Inc.'s balance sheet (Real Simple's parent company) leads me to believe this issue of timing is not an error. The company obviously is having issues (like all print-subscription companies). This may in fact be a way to prey on impatient subscribers who don't want to wait 2-3 weeks to receive their issue in the mail, even though they have already paid for the subscription.

When I inquired to Real Simple about the issue, they gave me what was obviously a company issued generic response about not having information about news stand delivery...it sounded like I was not the first to inquire about this due to the lack luster response and overall unwillingness to help.

To any husbands looking to purchase as a gift, make sure your wife has the patience to wait for her monthly issue - otherwise you will be paying for the subscription and paying for it at news stands as well. If you want to avoid any frustration, just reason that having her pay a premium at the news stand is worth the headache saved due to this mess.

title: How to live a "Real Simple" life if you have the money
text:
I was drawn to this magazine by the beautiful photography and promises of useful tips on everything from cleaning your kitchen to cheap gift ideas. And yes, there are a few interesting articles, tidbits, and suggestions, but I started to notice that a large portion of each issue is used for advertisements. And as many others have pointed out, there is a LOT of product placement within the articles/features themselves. And many of these recommended products are so expensive that I concluded that this magazine is targeted at wealthy housewives who can afford these things.
However, what I like most about this magazine are the recipes. I've cooked some really yummy meals that were featured in the cooking section and recently they've added a "shopping list" section that puts all the ingredients needed for the recipes in one shopping list. I bought the magazine for several months but unfortunately, the recipes alone were not worth the hefty price (and mostly empty content), so I stopped buying the magazine.
Defenitely NOT for the budget-minded!

title: Do yourself a favor and subscribe to Good Housekeeping instead
text:
I've subscribed to Real Simple for a year now and am not planning to renew. There is simply not much in this magazine (as the other reviewers have noted, there are a LOT of ads). If you want Real Simple tips, sign up for their emails, which often are precisely the same information in the magazine, but for free. There are a few good ideas in here, but I don't really know if it is worth the value of a subscription at the full price.

Also, from trying their recipes, I think that Good Housekeeping's are vastly superior. I'm a pretty avid cook (I also subscribe to Saveur, Bon Appetit, Cook's Country, and Cooks Illustrated) and I often find that there is something just slightly off with the recipes I make from Real Simple. Can't quite put my finger on why, but I'd definitely go to the other magazines first.

In general, Good Housekeeping is the better deal: more information, more articles, more (and better) recipes AND the Amazon price for that one is less than $8/year. I got a 3-year subscription for $20. You choose.

text: I am extremely shocked and disappointed at some of the content I have come across in Real Simple as of late; the August issue to be exact.  It seems that the magazine is not very well researched in some of the topics that it has chosen to write about such as the fact that infant formula equals that of human breast milk and is much easier and time-saving to feed a baby.  Unfortunately, their source, receives money for his research from the company that makes Enfamil baby formula...hummmmmmmmmm.  This kind of makes me wonder about all the sources that Real Simple refers to when writing on various topics.  Are they all suffering from a conflict of interest as this one obviously is?  Anyone who is up to date on what the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends (among countless other agencies and groups specializing in child nutrition and development) would know that breastfeeding is recommended for babies until AT LEAST one year of age.  And all these advocates for breastfeeding have countless facts and research proving the superior quality of nutrition to that of infant formula.  For example, did you know that pasteurized breast milk is written out in prescriptions for premature and sick babies and children in hospitals to heal them and keep them alive? Since Real Simple has proven to me that they use sketchy and biased sources and unreliable information regarding very important subject matter, I will not be buying or reading this magazine ever again and will strongly discourage everyone I know to [not read] it also.

title: On the fence
text:
I used to subscribe to Real Simple when it stayed true to its humbler origins. It was my favorite magazine to flip through for money-saving tips, "aha" features, thoughtful and well-written articles, and home-decorating and wardrobe inspiration.

On one hand, RS still has the features that I love and that can't be found in other magazines, or at least in such a neatly organized, consistent manner (for example, their feature of how to use common items for alternate uses, "best of" tests of products, 50 gifts under $50, etc). While many product suggestions have become pricier over the years, they do seem to throw in some low-budget options (the latest issue featured a pair of shoes from Payless, for example). Finally, the photography and artistry of the publication is an aesthetic I really appreciate.

On the other hand, I echo other people's sentiments. RS used to only feature a few ads. Now it consitutes every other page. I'm surprised that RS has lost touch with what I feel was its ultimate mission. Instead, it has franchised into TV shows and products that makes Real Simple a corporate brand and strayed from the grassroots-friendly, SIMPLE publication I fell in love with.

I'm crossing my fingers that the folks at Real Simple get it, and that a return back to the drawing board is in order.

I'm just glad I renewed at $5. Any more than that, and it would've been a waste.

title: Picture book with very little content: simple in a bad way!
text:
Recently got my first issue of a trial subscription (April, 2011). Other comments have already noted the miniscule article-to-ad ratio and heavily promoted mindless consumerism. I concur. "Articles" are really just giant photographs (pretty, yes, and perfectly commercial of course) with a few lines of jaunty text. I feel like it took a whole 15 minutes to read through the actual content of this very thick issue. I was hoping for something more meaty, less like a sequence of quippy billboards and more like the hints-from-Heloise tome I read as a kid.

In fact the picture-book layout felt rather infantilizing: a calming, pretty, grown-up version of kid-targeted loud ads for must-haves. It's not all commercial: one article consisted of picture diagrams for a handful of exercise moves, and I think there was a brief, lightweight interview somewhere in there. I know I shouldn't have expected much, but such terribly spare text content gives the impression they don't require their audience to know how to read! What a letdown.

title: Shallow, glib, and uninformative
text:
Like many other reviewers, I've been a subscriber to "Business Week" for a long time. I also subscribe to "The Economist" and "Barrons" - so that's where I'm coming from. And like many other reviewers, I have no plans to renew my subscription. The major reasons are below.

The magazine is biased. The mostly shallow analysis starts with a left of center and statist point of view that's jarring in a business magazine. It also doesn't seem like a particularly intelligent approach in a publication whose readers (at least those outside of Wall Steet and the banking industry not dependent on Uncle Sam's largesse) may not lean left, but I suspect the editors may not even be aware there are alternative viewpoints. I'm not a particularly political person, but the bias is noticeable and offputting. "Barrons" tilts to the right, but at least they're upfront about it.

The "Etc" section of the magazine is offensively vapid. Many of the articles are personality driven tributes to the rich and famous; other articles are odes to conspicuous consumption or fatuous exercises in filling magazine space. For example, in the issue in front of me (April 18, 2011), there's two pages on casting directors' choices of actors to play in an imaginary movie about Bernie Madoff. If that seems pointless to you, you probably don't want to be reading the new incarnation of "Business Week."

The magazine is full of cutting edge and colorful graphics that confuse rather than illuminate. Often, the lines on graphics run through and obscure the words in articles. That tendency came into full flower in the infamous year-end double issue which was a nightmare of graphics run wild.

Can't recommend this, unfortunately. I'll continue to pick up the occasional issue, and may resubscribe if it once again becomes an impartial business magazine. It's far from that now.

title: Love!
text: I've been getting this magazine for about 6 months, and I couldn't be happier. You get roughly 15 misses patterns (often more) per issue which is quite a bit of bang for your buck. Sizes generally range from 34-44 (US 8-18 pattern sizing), with several options for plus sizes (44-52). Each month, you will also find a wide range of other things to create, such as childrenswear, menswear, bags, home décor, toys, knit/crochet, etc. You name it, Burdastyle dabbles in it, but you just never know what you are going to get- each month is a surprise. As far as difficulty, Burdastyle is quite a bit different than US patterns. First of all, the pattern insert somewhat resembles a road map when you first unfold it. Each pattern piece must be traced off onto your own tissue paper and seam allowances are not included. Things that are rectangular in shape (like button plackets, cuffs) must be drafted yourself with the measurements they give you. You don't get very wordy, very specific instructions with diagrams. What you get is text that has been translated from German to UK English with NO pictures, other than the pattern layout. They do include 2 sewing lessons in each issue though, which includes pictures and step-by-step instructions. There is a page that has the line art for each design with a dot system that indicates difficulty, 1 dot meaning easy, and 3 (usually the highest) meaning more difficult. This is generally a good place to start if you are unsure. I highly recommend this to any sewing enthusiast, especially to those who have a good knowledge base and are looking for something new. The lines of these designs are very unique, interesting, and very trendy. I don't think you would be disappointed!

title: The best publication in its class, but not perfect
text:
Of the two major wine magazines, Wine Spectator and Wine Advocate, I have to say that Wine Advocate is my preferred source for finding a truly exceptional wine to enjoy. Wine Advocate is primarily the work of the noted wine critic Robert Parker, who is sometimes accused of being one of the leading "wine snobs" in the industry. Although Parker does use some pretentious lingo and some obscure references in his tasting notes, I find his tasting descriptions generally more accurate than those of the critics of Wine Spectator. Sure, he dislikes Burgundy, but at least now he has hired a more than competent fellow critic (Pierre Rovani) to cover that region for him.

Both Wine Spectator and Wine Advocate have been criticized for writing too many superlative reviews of less than exceptional wines, but I feel that Parker and Wine Advocate are less guilty in that respect, even though, as a previous reviewer noted, he does put more wines in the coveted 95+ point range. Still, Wine Advocate does a far better job than Wine Spectator of placing wines and their ratings in perspective, and avoiding clichés such as "vintage of a lifetime" that the Spectator frequently falls prey to. I have found Parker and Wine Advocate to be superior to Wine Spectator in their coverage of Bordeaux, especially in my favorite sub-regions, Sauternes and Barsac.

My only major complaints about Wine Advocate is that Parker generally assumes that all of his readers can afford to pay the relatively high price for his publication (currently more than $12/issue on Amazon). There are many 90+ point wines available for the difference between the yearly costs of Wine Advocate and Wine Spectator. Additionally, Parker and Wine Advocate really do not focus as much on wine values as they could, and I have found Parker's coverage of Australia somewhat disappointing. Generally speaking, however, I find Wine Advocate to be the best major Wine Publication available in English and would recommend it to anyone who enjoys wine with a passion.

title: Stereophile isn't for you
text:
There are some big problems with Stereophile that make it worse than useless unless you already know a lot about audio (so that you can separate the useful parts from the stuff they make up):

- There's a lot of misinformation, bias, opinion and pure fantasy mixed in to the articles. Unless you already know quite a bit about audio, it may be hard to separate the useful information from the rubbish.

The writers and the editors are simply not interested in really getting the facts right and testing what they know against reality - that's hard work and it's inconvenient, after all. And facing reality would get in the way of the real reason this magazine is published, which is ....

- Like most magazines, Stereophile is a vehicle for selling advertising. Though they like to believe otherwise, Stereophile is no different from GQ or Maxim or Elle magazines. (That shouldn't surprise you, even though it might.) Stereophile's main purpose is to help sell you more stuff, just like almost every other magazine.

And, like GQ or Elle, encouraging fashion trends is a key part of Stereophile trying to get you to spend more money. That, for example, is why they are so excited about the return of vinyl. It's not because vinyl actually sounds better (!?). It's because after years of stasis, it's a huge opportunity to sell more advertising to try to sell you more stuff. The fact that they moved all the turntables, etc, to the front of their recommended list of equipment helps prove the point. Fashion trends are a magazine's best friend, whether it's GQ or Stereophile.

By the way, I'm not suggesting that the writers are consciously slanting the articles. In a way, it's far more insidious than that: they actually believe what they write. There's an implicit selection process - the only way to get hired to or stay on the staff at Stereophile is to drink the Kool Aid. Over time the primary goal has become making money, so Stereophile has inevitably been shaped into a vehicle for selling advertising.

So keep in mind that Stereophile isn't published for you, it's published for the advertisers and the owners. That might help guide you through the quagmire that is Stereophile magazine. You're simply the "target" demographic. Hold on to your wallet, and decide what to buy with your ears, not your eyes.

title: Far superior in quality and format to the US version.
text: The US version of Country Living should aspire to the quality of content and articles offered in the UK version.  I suspect there may be a demographics issue -- in the US, the notion of "Country" has been hijacked by animals (ie: geese, ducks, cows, rabbits) wearing trailing bows, grape-vine wreaths with plastic flowers hot-glued on, and tole painted milk jugs.  When I think American "Country Living" I think "Buy One Mobile Home, Get One Free:  Furniture Included".  In the UK, Country Living feels a bit more authentic and less kitsch-y.  There are great articles about animal husbandry, local food initiatives (as well as guidance on DIY food production), gorgeous old restored farmhouses and the shabby chic furniture that fills them, charming commentaries and columns detailing the quirky and quaint vignettes that make up a *life actually lived in the countryside* and filled with country pursuits.  Even the format (large) and quality of the paper (glossy, as opposed to National Enquirer quality) is superior.  I'm a firm believer in "You get what you pay for," and in this case, that is certainly true.

title: Change to Food featured in Cooking Light
text: I’ve been subscribing to cooking light for 8-9 years. I have accumulated many great recipes from cooking light over the years. There has always been a huge variety of recipes to try, from easy /super fast weeknight dinners to themed meals (I.e recipes using anti-inflammatory ingredients) or entire holiday menus, reader recipes, and how-to techniques. I mean, one issue of cooking light would really give you so much to be inspired by and to be educated on. The magazine has changed editors, from Scott Mowbray to Hunter Lewis in 2014. The magazine still has great articles on food and health and still is inspiring - but there has been a noticeable change is the type of food and recipes that it features. I’m findng it harder to choose recipes that I want to cook. The style of food is going in a direction where it is very heavy on vegetables. I just don’t find the food as appealing, as it seems to focus on food you should eat if you are on a diet as opposed to food you want to eat that happens to also be fresh and healthy. It’s lost it’s “oh my gosh that looks yummy” reaction to “hmm that’s an interesting looking salad.” Some people will love the change but I personally find the food to be one-note. The photography has never been better and the health and food journalism continues to shine. Any food article written by Ann Taylor Pittman will be excellent. But the food featured in Cooking Light seems to have lost its yum factor. I really hope it is a temporary phase.

title: This magazine used to be great
text: Shape used to be such a great magazine. They used to have detailed workout plans for cardio, strength training, and diet that were excellent, creative, and challenging with amazing photography. I remember their beach body workouts that were a part of an ongoing 5 month series and their total body workout plans that would be kicked off in January issues. Every issue would be full of cardio and  strength training plans, along with express workouts and specific moves for arms, abs, etc.This magazine used to be so inspiring! Now when I flip through it, I actually get mad at how little this magazine invests in giving their readers a real workout plan. The magazine likes to write articles about the art of exercising but with little to no tangible exercise examples. It drives me nuts to get teased with a picture of a person working out only to turn the next page and see text descriptions of what to do. Seriously? This is a fitness magazine and you can’t provide a picture of the exercise you are recommending, you want me to read a text description of what to do? Another annoyance I find is how Shape will feature pages and pages of glamorous fitness models posing and flexing their lean muscles in trendy workout clothes, along with text describing how great a workout you are going to have. After eagerly turning the page to reach the actual workout ‘section’, I see one page crammed with tiny photos. Shape will only dedicate a single page to the exercises after the huge buildup. They don’t even lay out the exercise photos with enough space to separate out the moves, they are smashed together and shrunk down. Also, the exercises are not that attainable - some of the moves are complicated but with the limited photos, you are left puzzling over how to move from step 1 to 2. And that is only if you get any kind of exercise plan. I’ve just flipped through a years worth of Shape mags that I have been needing to recycle, and it is not predictable to see any workout plan laid out per issue. If you enjoy reading about exercising, but not interested in actually doing it, then this mag is fine. But I wish Shape would make big changes to their direction. I am so profoundly disappointed in what it has become and will no longer subscribe to Shape.

title: Just another pop-science magazine--and with bad customer support
text:
I have been reading SciAm since the 1970s. However, in the past decade or so, the dumbing down of this once fine monthly has made it orbit between decent to just another pop-science magazine, such as "Discover." Since I travel internationally, I am only able to subscribe to SciAm digitally. I hear that "American Scientist" is much better. Alas, "American Scientist" does not have a digital subscription.
FURTHER UPDATE: In the past five years I have held two SciAm digital subscriptions. I cancelled my first subscription because too often it was difficult to download given issues I had paid for. After a one-year hiatus, I subscribed again, hoping things were better. I have again cancelled— this time because not only was it difficult to find my download, but the SciAm site refused to let me download the June 2016 issue into my iPad. Whereas other newspapers and magazines I subscribe to or use have a "Sign In" or "Log On" link—usually top right—on their home landing page, SciAm has a only "Subscribe" button. One has to search around inside the website to find the Log On button. Since I don't always remember where to look for the Log On button, I sometimes click on the issue jpg to bring me to the issue page. One would think a paying customer who is signed in would have the option of downloading the issue here. But NO! Here you will only find options to "subscribe," or "pay" for a single issue or article. When I was unable to download the June 2016 issue on the archive page, which I had found with difficulty, I made an overseas call to Scientific American's service department to ask where and how I could download my issue. I was told to hit the "Store" button on the main page and to hit the "Archive" button on the Store page.( Apparently, Scientific American has such little regard for paying customers that they want to try to sell them something additional before letting them get what they've already paid for.) I was then told to click on the June 2016 issue to download. I still couldn't download the issue. The rep took my email address and said SciAm's tech department would get back. Two days later I received an email from Scientific American trying to sell me my already paid for June 2016 issue. I have since canceled my subscription.
