title: Backpacker: Destinations, Skills, Gear
text:
Backpacker magazine is for great resource for adventurers, hikers, campers, trekers, and gear-heads.

Backpacker is a quick read (generally apx 80-100 pages)with colorful fullpage vista photos, which features:
- adventure narratives
- trip specifics: GPS routes, maps, permit info, trail highlights, elevation stats, etc
- lists of the "greats" (enumerated lists of great camping sites, great gear, great national parks, etc)
- recipes for the trail
- gear recommendations
- survival skill guides
- additional information/resources made available on the webiste

The destination guide information is helpful to expand your backpacking, camping, and trekking trip options. The skills are sometimes pretty basic (first aid, bear safety, leave no trace)--but even highly-accomplished adventurers can use a reminder sometimes. The gear suggestions are often of the expensive-cutting-edge persuasion and trend toward the pursuit of the hyper-light.

title: Shopshop
text:
Ok, first of all, to settle the skinny-model debate, truth is that fashions spreads are shot way before they appear in the magazine so only samples of the clothes are available then. Fashion samples come exclusively in sizes 5 to 7 (or used to last time I checked) so it takes a model that is a 5 to 7 to model them. Also, in Lucky's defense I have to say that A LOT of their fashion pictures feature only the clothes laid out with no one wearing them, but anyway...

As far as the magazine goes, I enjoy it. Since it devotes itself entirely to shopping, it gives great advice on fashion, beauty, and home decorating. To be honest with you, I'd become disillusioned with other magazines as far as fashion went (No Cosmo, sadly I don't wear green satin gym short shorts with stilettos to the office) and the fashion Lucky presents seems far more real. True, I still find the occasional "I'd never wear that" item but mostly I find great tips for dressing either up or down, office or weekend. It's great. More than anything, it works amazingly well as a shopping companion what with some more affordable stores are coming out with great items, Lucky along with its "Yes" and "Maybe?" tags is great to take along and copy a few looks for a lot less. Some people have given some very negative reviews but they should realize that this magazine works as a guide, not a rulebook.

The Beauty section is good but not great and certainly not that different from Beauty sections found in any other magazine of this type. I'm not gonna remark so much on it except I enjoy the previews of new products.

The home decorating part I really enjoy. For the most part, the looks they propose are neutral and pretty Still, they find a few looks that are more daring and I'm certain a lot of people are eager to try. No matter the looks you choose, decorating in this manner is way easy to emulate at home.

With so many areas where to glean useful advice, this is agreat all-around magazine. Obviously if you don't enjoy shopping, this is not the maagzine for you but still fun to look at. Whether you enjoy following its advice or taking it shopping with you or not, Lucky makes for a well-rounded shopping chica!

title: Like reading Playboy for the articles
text:
This is NOT your typical girly magazine. I mean that, however, in the best way possible. It gets to the reader on (some) pretense of fashion, celebrities, and makeup but is really, really a smart read. If you're the quintessential girly girl, it might catch you with its gossip and fashion photo spreads, you'll end up loving it for its "mind", though. No one's too fat in here, no makeup "must-have's", no gimmicks to getting him to love you. Nope, just stuff a little bit deeper in here.
The articles are definitely the best part of this magazine. I've seen everything covered here from politics to perfume testing. It's like no girly magazine you've ever seen before. They do have the usual gossip and trends but put forth in a much more thought-provoking way any smart girl will end up, if not loving, at least liking enough.
They also have the celebrity issue every year where celebrities come together to "produce" most of the magazine. It's quite refreshing to see what these people can come up with, usually with very funny results.
I gotta admit I'm not a subscriber but I do pick it up from time to time. It's a fun, smart detour from the usual Cosmo. Buy it for the fluff, love it for its mind.

title: Good food fast
text:

The format of this magazine is like a really great cookbook. Every recipe has a picture, is very clearly stated with its ingredients and steps of the procedure, even nutrition information and it also includes useful tips on measuring, ingredient substitution and the like.
The recipes range from old classics to trendy new stuff to try if you've got adventurous tastebuds. I completely love it and experiment thoroughly with it. I recommend that you try it too sometime.
My only complaint, if any, is that they sometimes get carried away suggesting the use of Pillsbury products as main ingredients, if you can't find one or an acceptable substitute, you can't go on! However, it's infrequent that they do so and in no way a reason not to subscribe to this great magazine.

title: Not the Country Living I Used to Love
text: I've finally gotten around to reading the April 2019 issue and sadly it has solidified my decision to cancel my subscription. I fell in love with this magazine while in my 20s. I love to decorate, but being young and poor, I needed to find a style that could be had on a stretched dollar. Country Living fit the bill. I loved everything about it, and felt I could easily replicate the style on a budget. I greedily read every issue as soon as it was delivered and saved every issue for future perusing. Then the editor left and I didn't quite gel with the new one. But the magazine was still good, you could still rely on it for inspiration. I learned to enjoy the new editor's style and happily continued my subscription. And then she left too. The current magazine has become tone deaf. The young 20 something that could actually visualize the pages coming to life in her own home, despite a meager budget, has become a jaded 30 something that no longer sees herself among the pages. You can no longer recreate the pages in CL in your home unless you've got a lot of money to spend. And others who complain about the ads are right, it's ridiculous how many pages are devoted to ads. The style is cluttered and the monthly features are boring. The current April 2019 issue is especially insulting. How many of your readers can just drop their day job and start an organic farm, an antique shop, a vineyard, a flower farmer, etc? It's become so elitist and I'm just a small town country girl, in need of some new inspiration.

title: Content, where's the content?
text:
I USED to love this magazine. It had great, usable recipes and lots of wine knowledge to expose the reader to. Now it seems desperately lacking in content. Today I counted the pages of writing to the pages of ads. The ratio was about 1 to 2 (i.e. about double the number of pages of ads over the pages of content).

What content there was often included huge photos with a single sentence to introduce a story (taking a whole page up to introduce a story that was sometimes 1-3 pages in total). Other times content was "food romance", which is my own term. By that I mean things such as describing a writer's adoration and experiences with riesling or items that writers/editors think are nifty, or a cultural scene in a specific city. While not totally unwelcome by me, these "food romance" articles feel like filler, and recipes and information on wines seem to fall by the wayside. Recipes end up shifted to the back of the magazine in a clump, and are much less inspiring than those found in cookbooks that simply lay them out with a photo for most/each recipe.

The biggest fault I find with the magazine is that the advertisements are often disguised as content, potentially, but not always with the word "advertisement" written discretely on the page.

When it's hard to even FIND the content in a magazine, it's time to switch to a better magazine. I'll be on the lookout for a replacement to my good old Food and Wine. (I've been happy with Cook's Illustrated and Wine Spectator).

title: Pseudoscience, snake oil magazine
text: My title pretty much sums up stereophile, when i got into audio i use to think this was a reliable source to hi fi audio. Once i actually learned the science behind audio reproduction I relalized that this magazine was pretty much (in the words of our vice president) a bunch of malarkey. Reviewing expensive cables, interconnects, AC power cables, cable lifters, vinyl and CD demagnitizers, and the outrageous claims they make about each one is asinine. Most of their reviews are done in different rooms which already is going to make loudspeakers sound different, and also done without double blind testing. Most of what they publish in the reviews is plecebo effect, of course if you swap a $40 dollar cable with a $2000 cable its going to sound better to you because you are expecting it to sound better. After all its $1960 more! Every single human being is susceptible to plecebo effect which is why it is imperative to isolate any visul, and price difference bias from the reviewer. It is done in the medical field with new medicine but not in high end audio. The other things they do just borderline on insanity, for example they reviewed the vinyl and CD demagnitizer and claimed it actually improved the sound but of course fail to provide any evidence of this. Any person who passed high school science class will tell you that this is complete nonsence, CDs are made of polycarbonate plastic and vinyl is made of thermoplastic polymer or PVC. Both materials do NOT magnitize. Another is AC power cords costing 2 or 3 thousand dollars which they review and of course say it made a profound difference in the sound. Which again does not hold water in a court of science, its a power cable and audio does not pass through it. What good is 2-3 feet of so called "good" power cable going to do when you got normal copper cable in your walls? These are just a few examples I could go on and on. I rarely see them talk about room treatment which actually makes a profound difference and is backed up by science and measurements. If you want to really learn about how to set up a TRUE hifi system in your house i recommend two books, one is floyd toole's book called sound reproduction, the the other is by ethan winer called the audio expert. Both are fantastic books that cut out the snake oil charlatans and get down to what REALLY matters and to what makes a audible difference.

If you're a gay guy with diverse interests, I'd highly recommend DNA magazine instead. They are based in Australia but somehow manage to be much more relevant and interesting to someone like me. title: Once Decent Magazine Has Degenerated Into Maxim (Golf Edition)
text:
.
1.5 Stars

I've subscribed to Golf Digest (GD) for most of the past two decades but stopped paying for it a few years back; I've been getting a year's subscription as an included freebie with entrance to my annual local golf expo. However, I've been skimming and skipping more and reading less of the magazine each year for the past half dozen years and it has deteriorated so much that I'd never bother spending a penny on it these days - it has become inundated with a strange blend of tabloid journalism and snobbish pseudo-sophistication that has tremendously diluted any useful or interesting content about the sport of golf.

Think of some of the worst things about the sport of golf. Over the past five or so years, Golf Digest has actually been PROMOTING many of those negative aspects.

Let's take the male-dominated chauvinism of the sport, as the primary example. A lot of women are turned off by what they see as a sport primarily played by men who primarily are happy with the status quo of few women participants in the sport. Anyone who doubts that this is still the case should go to a typical golf course on a weekend - one will see at least a 5-to-1 ratio of male to female golfers, maybe even a much higher ratio - there have been plenty of times I've played here in the upper Midwest on a Saturday or Sunday when the only female on the course was the beer cart girl. What has GD done to appeal to women golfers, to address the sport of golf from a women's perspective? Other than have a cover photo in a recent issue of a shirtless Rory McIlroy posing as a Greek god, practically nothing.

Some years back, Golf Digest made available to subscribers a special women's golf insert to the magazine that could be included in one's issues if the subscriber requested it. I requested it for my wife and daughter and never received a single copy with that women's golf insert nor do I recall hearing anything further about it. Perhaps the publisher decided to cancel this option almost instantly figuring that if few people responded after maybe only a one-time notice of the option, that it wasn't of interest to anyone, rather than give reasonable notice and then see how many people wanted to take advantage of the optional content.

I haven't sat down with several years worth of GD issues and done a specific count, but I would guess that at most, half of the issues even mention the LPGA Tour or have any content on an LPGA golfer, and if there is such content, it is generally limited to maybe two pages; in contrast, every issue features interviews or articles about at least two PGA golfers and tips and pointers from three to four more. Several times a year the instructional pages will contain a tip from an LPGA touring pro or female club pro. But that's it for content addressed to women. My elementary school-aged daughter loves golf and I've tried to get her to read Golf Digest whenever I've received a new copy, hoping it will keep her interest in the sport high. A few times she's sat down, flipped through the magazine, and said "Dad, this is just about men golfers." I'll point out an interview with an LPGA golfer or instructional tip from a female teaching pro (generally never both in the same issue, though) and her response was "That's two pages out of ... what, maybe 150 pages? This magazine is for boys." You know what? She's 100% correct.

Golf Digest's decision essentially to ignore women golfers and include the barest modicum of female content necessary to avoid a label of completely male-centered, is really short-sighted. What sort of person subscribes to a golf magazine? That's right, golfers and fans of professional golf. The most fertile source of new subscribers to an activity-based magazine is those who are new to the activity - the magazine will certainly increase its subscriber base if it promotes the activity. The largest untapped source of new golfers and thus new golf magazine subscribers is women, yet Golf Digest virtually ignores the entire gender, and avoids a chance to grow both the sport and their subscriber base [* FN 1] And for that matter, once the initial Tiger Woods decade subsided, GD has virtually ignored minorities in the sport of golf.

Sadly, the most prominence Golf Digest has given to women has been in their annual skin.. err... fitness issue, where for the past three years they have featured a scantily clad and attractive female on the cover who is supposedly promoting greater "fitness" among golfers. Two year ago it was arrogant, snappy, and plastic surgery-enhanced former Golf Channel personality Holly Sonders and last year it was model Paulina Gretzky whose tenuous connection to golf is that she is the fiancée of PGA golfer Dustin Johnson. Rather pathetically, unless a woman shoots a 58 in a tournament or wins a calendar-year grand slam - two or three LPGA majors in one year aren't necessarily enough, ask outrageously talented but less-than svelte Inbee Park how much attention she received from GD after winning not one or two but THREE LPGA majors in 2013 - it's not likely she will be featured in her sport's so-called premier magazine. A woman has a better chance of appearing in Golf Digest or on the magazine's website if she's a pretty WAG (wives and girlfriends)of a PGA Tour player than a remarkably skilled LPGA Tour player. Hell, I bet Amanda Dufner, the very pretty soon-to-be ex-wife of frumpy PGA Championship winner Jason Dufner, has received as much coverage in the magazine and in the magazine's website as any current or future LPGA hall of fame player over the past half decade.

Amid outcry that the magazine is objectifying women and ignoring actual female athletes, this year the "fitness" issue features 20 year-old American star Lexi Thompson, a four-time LPGA Tour winner including a major last summer, as its cover model. Problem addressed, right? Golf Digest would have to be freakin' obtuse to screw up that choice of a cover model, wouldn't they? Well, indeed, the publishers at Golf Digest are just that dumb. They had Lexi posed topless. OK, she does have a small towel draped over her shoulders that covers the center of her breasts, but otherwise, she's naked from the waist up. My family and I are big Lexi Thompson fans - three summers ago, we attended an LPGA major and followed her for the whole 18 holes. How the hell am I supposed to show my daughter a major story on her favorite golfer when Golf Digest chose to show her nearly nude in a cover photo meant to appeal to randy male readers??

I honestly think that the publishing crew and senior editors at Golf Digest either came over straight from Maxim magazine or are a bunch of middle-aged dufuses (or is the plural of dufus spelled "dufi"?) who desperately want to be hip-and-trendy and think their subscription woes are caused not by people going to digital sources rather than hard copy magazines, but by the lack of "racy" content. The annual skin/fitness covers drive away women readers and who do they attract? For every guy at a train station or airport news kiosk who is looking for something to read on his commute who might grab the "fitness" issue, at least another one will buy Sports Illustrated instead, not wanting to be seen reading a "skin rag" in public. It's pretty well known among males of puberty age or older that the internet is overflowing with graphic imagery of a purile nature, so I doubt a single guy has decided to subscribe to GD thinking "I've been looking for a source for photos of scantily-clad females and until now I've not been able to find one, I've always thought that golf was a fuddy-duddy sport, but this cover story has changed my mind! Ring me up as a new Golf Digest subscriber!"

Online right now on GD's website there is an instructional article featuring a tip from Blair O'Neal, one of the more famous women in the world of golf, and certainly not among the most skilled. Hmm, Blair O'Neal, an LPGA star you are asking? Nope. She's got no bio on the LPGA site (and they retain bios of pretty much anyone who played a regular season in the past 15 to 20 years or so - the head pro of one local course played on the LPGA Tour for a few years back in the 90's earning not much more than enough to cover her travel expenses and she's still listed on the LPGA website) nor does she have a Wikipedia page, which nearly all athletes of any even modest level of accomplishment have. So who the heck is she? O'Neal was a contestant on several seasons of the Golf Channel's reality golf competition show The Big Break who is best known not for winning anything (I spent but a minute looking but found nothing to suggest she's made the cut of a single LPGA event if she even played in any, likely on sponsors exemptions because of her semi-celebrity status). Blair O'Neal is known for being cute, blond, leggy, and posing in a bikini in the opening credits introducing the season's Big Break contestants. We have several hundred present and past female golfers who actually have accomplished something by earning and keeping an LPGA Tour card, yet not one of those athletes, who, unlike Blair O'Neal, actually are world-class golfers who have accomplished something in the sport of golf, were deemed by Golf Digest to be worthy of consultation on golf instruction. Yep, for Golf Digest, easy on the eyes in a short skirt is more important than actual knowledge and expertise.

I did just recall one article in the magazine in which they sent a cute female staffer who owned at least one tight tee-shirt undercover to work as a beer cart girl and surprisingly, did report rather candidly that the typical sort of guy such female golf course employees encounter (the pompous, windbag sort of Golf Guy who ironically is the target audience of Golf Digest) is quite a tool. But that hardly is an article of interest to women who like the sport of golf and quite frankly I think the main reason it got published was some boss at Golf Digest took a look at his intern or staff member's chest and said to himself "We've got to think of some way to get that published in this magazine!"

So not only does Golf Digest essentially ignore, if not offend, women golfers, but they also ignore families who like to play golf. I think I can recall a single article in all the years I've read and received Golf Digest that addresses how to further one's children's interest in the sport (and the more I think of it, the more I believe I could very well be mistaken and it was actually an article about kids in Tennis magazine that is coming to mind). Multiple issues a year address "golf buddy" trips to Myrtle Beach the Upper Peninsula, etc..., but in the history of the magazine, not a single article has ever appeared on destinations for a family golf trip with children nor have they ever done a single article or list of teaching pros who specialize in teaching kids or done any instructional articles aimed at kids.

The publishers of Golf Digest are not targeting the typical golfer, they are targeting "Golf Guy," a male golfer possessing multiple negative aspects in various subfields of arrogance and snobbery. There are a multitude of Golf Guys on any online golf forum, they all add about 20-70 yards onto the length of their average drives as they boast about their games, they all claim to be low and mid-handicap players and claim that any person who isn't physically and mentally capable of breaking 90 regularly or who loses more than a ball or two per round is a pathetic hack who should stick to the range and not clutter-up and slow down the course for "real" golfers (forgetting that fewer than 10% of all golfers shoot in the 80s or lower). Golf Guy arrogantly dismisses complaints about the cost of the sport, claiming a $75 greens fee is a "bargain." A typical Golf Guy will claim to finish a round easily in two hours or less (virtually impossible without rushing frantically, on a wide-open course and without possessing near-scratch playing ability), he claims he plays at least 3 to 4 rounds per week and will make disparaging comments about the lack of time-management skills of anyone who states they cannot play as frequently. However, unless Golf Guy is entertaining clients on the course regularly or is taking his kids to the course with him, he's not a parent or isn't much of one at all, neglecting his family for his hobby if he is playing that often, given how time-intensive the game of golf generally is.

If you've played enough golf, you've seen plenty of Golf Guys on the course - they're the ones wearing wool dress pants on a 95*F day because "they respect the traditions of the game," they pseudo-respectfully refer to famous golfers and treat them as gods (even long-dead or more populist ones or ones who were arrogant horse's arses [** FN2]) as "Mister Hogan" or "Mister Palmer" or "Mr. Nicklaus." The typical Golf Guy was the first one wearing dorky white belts when that silly 70's style revived, and he wouldn't be caught dead in less than a $150 Bobby Jones golf shirt with anything less than the latest model of $500 driver, $300 putter and $1,000 set of irons, all top-tier brands, in his bag. I once got paired up with a Golf Guy when I walked-on to a golf course and I asked him what he was doing when I saw him snooping into my golf bag. He responded "I like to know what sort of equipment a man has before I play him for money." I responded "I don't gamble and if I did, why would you think I'd play someone like you for money anyway?" What a *(&%@&()@! I am positive he's been enjoying Golf Digest a whole lot these past several years.

Golf Digest's publishers have decided to cater to Golf Guy's snobbish whims and fancies in the past few years, so the magazine regularly features reviews of $70,000 to $100,000 luxury cars (this is related to golf because ... because apparently nothing less will hold two sets of golf clubs in the trunk nor be able to navigate to any local golf course ??), they have had multiple featured style articles on watches priced from $3,000 to $20,000 (because nothing less will enable a "real" golfer to get to his tee time promptly? Yet aren't most of these same guys claiming that no "real" golfer could hit a quality shot with the distraction of anything appearing on his wrist?), and they have other "golf style" articles that feature expensive, pretentious clothing, shoes, even cigars. To make Golf Guy feel like he's a really thoughtful, conscientious type of guy, GD includes a monthly column "Golf Saved Me!" with some sappy, feel-good, do-gooder tripe of a human interest story relating vaguely to golf.

Golf Digest does publish a lot of golf tips and instructional columns and articles including a monthly one by Tom Watson. Over the years I've read hundreds of these golf tips and I've come to realize a few things as I learn more about the game of golf. First, there are not one or two ways to skin the proverbial golf cat, there are many. There are probably a dozen or two or three different ways to impart moderate amounts of desirable left-to-right or right-to-left spin to hit a draw or fade and there are at least an equal number of ways to reduce excess spin to avoid the dreaded hooking and slicing. Second, I don't think many so-called golf instructional experts understand golf as well as they pretend and third, I don't think most of those golf instructors are as clear of communicators as they think they are. Out of those hundreds of golf tips, I can recall and remember about five that have actually helped: aim right side of fairway but swing parallel to dead center to hit a draw; stand with feet closer than shoulder length for pitches; scoop out a dollar bill-sized divot hitting sand first for bunker shots; take 2 clubs more, position ball back by right foot, take 3/4 swing for knock-down shots into the wind; and after calculating break on the green, add at least 1/3 more, as amateurs chronically underestimate break. Out of hundreds of tips, I should have been able to retain more knowledge and to the extent that my learning style for sports is not to blame, I attribute this failing to a) often mediocre, less-than-completely-clear writing in instructional articles; and b) lack of editorial consistency - some of these various tips on how to cure a slice, for instance, are simply not consistent with each other. While golf is probably the most complex of all sports to understand and master, I have retained and utilized a significantly greater portion of the instructional articles I've read in Tennis and Ski magazine, for instance and have found them more clearly written and useful, than those that appear in Golf Digest.

Golf Digest's equipment "reviews" have fluctuated in content but are of minimal worth. At times they are of the "Here's some marketing synopses on the latest drivers, iron sets, putters and balls coming out this year" and during other periods they have supposed play-test reviews; I'll confess I cannot recall from the most recent equipment issue if they are presently doing just the "Here's what our advertisers tell us to print" or if they are in the phase where they do alleged reviews of the equipment. Either way, the substantial majority of equipment they review/highlight is made by their largest advertisers and other than golf balls, it is always high-end equipment. Despite the fact that the majority of people getting into the game of golf start out with some sort of modest-priced beginner's all-in-one set, they have never, ever done a comparison of say the typical $150 to $300 sets by Wilson, Dunlop, Top Flite, Adams, etc... nor compared them to higher end clubs (i.e. they are doing the car magazine equivalent of reviewing only Porches, BMWs, Cadillacs, and Ferraris, without a single review of an Accord, Camry or even a Civic or Escort). Nor has GD ever done even a single article on how to select used equipment, particularly an used set for a beginner (often a better option because the 1st and 2nd tier equipment actually does hit straighter and longer than cheap beginner sets). Maybe if several of the big online auction sellers of used golf clubs took out full page ads in GD this would change.

I have a problem with Golf Digest ball tests because they appear to be based solely on snobbishness and reputation of the ball manufacturer - in fact, the ball reviews are called the "Hot List: Golf Balls" - what matters is what is "hot" - i.e. trendy, not necessarily what works the best. Accordingly to Golf Digest, if it's small, round and has a "Titleist" logo on it, it's an automatic inclusion into the Hot List! as a best-of-the-best product in every price range, something that does not correlate to my experiences at all playing with that brand of balls. Let me admit that there is an excellent reason why more touring pros play Titleist Pro-V1 and Pro-V1x than all other balls combined - from my experience and that of every other good golfer (well, I'm too inconsistent to be called "good" but I do make a lot of good shots) I know, Pro-V1s do go the longest and have the best feel and spin on the greens of any ball on the market - they really are the best. However, I have found that all of Titleist's other, cheaper balls are mediocre performers against other similarly-priced balls, yet invariably, without exception, ever, GD rates all Titleist balls, not just the deserving Pro-V1s, as 5/5-star/gold-rated products.

I also don't care for Golf Digest's social tone, beyond just the snobbery about non-golf accessories and luxury items. This month's cover story is about long-hitting (both of the ball and allegedly the drug pipe) PGA star Dustin Johnson who recently came off a supposed self-imposed hiatus from the game while he "addressed some aspects of his personal life," which he has not specified but apparently has not denied the generally-accepted statements that he was in treatment for polysubstance abuse. There is also a fairly credible bit of information floating around that Johnson has for years had a cocaine problem, he failed a tour drug test, it was not his first time failing such a test, and his break from playing was actually a secret PGA Tour suspension. There are also supposedly reputable rumors that Johnson had been shagging the wife of one of his fellow Tour members, ending their marriage; gee, Tiger-haters, how do you reconcile your love of Johnson with your hatred of Tiger in light of their at minimum equivalent marriage-wrecking adultery? While I am glad that Johnson has straightened out his life to the point that he's playing well again, I don't think he deserves a cover story in Golf Digest nor the sympathy he's receiving from Golf Guy and Golf Digest unless he comes clean, admits his addictions, and starts to doing anti-drug promotions. Most iterations of Golf Guy are probably willing to forgive and hero-worship Dustin Johnson but loathe and will never forgive Tiger Woods, who longtime contributing GD writer Dan Jenkins recently lampooned quite obnoxiously in the magazine for his indiscretions [*** FN3], which I believe represents the sentiments of the magazine hiding behind a curmudgeonly journalistic legend. You see, Johnson is engaged to a blond beauty and committed the less-than-fully-pleasant-and-not-quite-socially-acceptable act of buying illegal substances sold by criminal syndicates who murder thousands of innocent people each year, whereas Woods committed the much more heinous crime of, first, being a person of color marrying a beautiful, naturally blond woman (even worse than if she was an unnatural blond) and second, cheating on her multiple times, most atrociously with women who were for the most part less attractive than his naturally blond, blue-eyed wife. While Tiger Woods is the biggest star the sport has probably ever known, I am confident that there are plenty of other PGA stars whose marriages ended because a cocky athlete always on the road was unfaithful, yet because those other stars were white, Golf Digest took no notice of them.

The magazine is not altogether worthless, though, because of the pro-tour golfer content. I do read many of the interviews of PGA (and the rare LPGA) star, which tend to be pretty well-written. I like the "What's In My Bag" monthly column where they show a photo of a PGA or very occasionally an LPGA touring pro's bag and clubs and we get the details and story behind why he is playing which equipment and what little superstitious item he carries for good luck. And there's a couple of semi-regular articles written by one or more anonymous journeyman PGA pros that supposedly candidly say what is right, wrong, and/or interesting about playing on the PGA Tour that a non-touring pro might not have realized. Finally, the magazine will usually include a pretty detailed and sometimes interesting article on whichever course is on this year's rotation for the U.S. Open, British Open (no, Golf Guy, it's not "THE Open" any more than UVA is "THE University" or OSU is "THE Ohio State University") or PGA Championship and that provides a nice background if I've got the time to sit down that weekend and watch some golf.

In conclusion, this magazine was never perfect but it has really deteriorated over the past half decade. The magazine essentially ignores women, completely ignores integrating kids into the sport, and increasingly has focused on a whole lot of content that really has nothing to do with the sport of golf from either the perspective of an amateur playing the sport or a fan of the professional tours. Golf Digest caters to the sort of guy who boasts about his healthy lifestyle and respect for family values, yet likes to sneak off to smoke cigars in the nudie bars, who boasts how generous he is as he tips the cute-but-inattentive waitress 30% while leaving barely 5% for the outstanding but plain and overweight woman who waits his table the next night. If the phrase "arrogant, snobby putz" can accurately be applied to you and you like golf, well, Golf Digest will be just your cup of tea. It's been a couple of years since I last subscribed to Golf magazine, but I remember it equaling in most ways Golf Digest's strengths or mediocrities and not having the issues and weaknesses such as promoting male chauvinism or snobbery like Golf Digest so blatantly does, so I'd recommend Golf over Golf Digest.

FOOTNOTES:

[* FN1] However, for any honest person wanting to talk about gender inequality in sports, one of the several fingers that most deserve to be pointed must be pointed squarely at women themselves. If it's not figure skating, gymnastics or diving, most (but not all) women, if given control of the remote, won't watch sports on television, not men's sports, not women's sports, not any kind of sports. When I attended an LPGA major a few years back, not counting families and heterosexual couples, groups of male fans there outnumbered female fans by a 2 to 1 margin, at least. I've also attended quite a few Div. I women's basketball, volleyball and hockey games over the years and there are always more male fans in the seats than female fans. Next time you watch a WTA match on television, you'll see more men in the stands than women and Anna Kournikova retired years ago.

[** FN2] Golf Guy's reverence, even hero-worship, of a number of golf legends not just as athletes but as people in general makes very little sense. Ben Hogan was by any reasonable person's standards an aloof, unpleasant person who routinely gave snarky non-answers to questions from journalists or fellow golf pros alike and screwed over a friend of his, who lost a position as a golf pro at a prestigious country club because Hogan failed to send in letter of recommendation. Just last week while sitting in a guest role commenting on the Player's Championship, John Feinstein (who might possess more current knowledge about golf and the PGA tour than any journalist alive), knowingly referred to Jack Nicklaus and Tom Watson as "not nice people."

[*** FN3] For many years Golf Digest featured a commentary column by covering-the-PGA-since-the-dawn-of-time sports journalist Dan Jenkins, who for reasons that are unknown to me, is lauded and revered by probably 99.9% of the Golf Guy community. Jenkins was friends with Hogan and knew all of the legends of golf during the middle of the 20th century and his specialty, aside from his access to all of these golf stars and legends, was his allegedly brilliant wit. To me, Jenkins was to sports humor what Carrottop is to regular humor or graphic stories of deer hunting would be to romance on a first date with a PETA member. He's the sort of crusty, pompous old goat who might call someone an idiot for claiming cigarettes are unhealthy or declare someone is "un-American" for stating that the legislature's attempt to pass laws promoting religion in schools violates the First Amendment (these are just hypotheticals, not actual examples that specifically and accurately can be attributed to Jenkins, but I wouldn't be even slightly surprised if they actually were applicable). For quite a while Jenkins seems to have taken a sabbatical and/or retired, but a few months back he published in Golf Digest a snarky, pseudo-clever "interview" with Tiger Woods, who will not in fact talk with or grant Jenkins a real-life interview because of some past comment or another. Woods got all upset and by foolishly going online in protest, guaranteed that a washed-up, bitter old has-been got triple the readership his article otherwise would have received. Jenkins despises Tiger Woods and while I have no proof of it, I'd bet at least a pet, if not a future grandchild, that if Tiger was blond and blue-eyed, Jenkins wouldn't have much, if any, problem with him; it's awfully hard for an old leopard to change his spots, few white octogenarian Texans have always been open-minded about dark skinned peoples, and nothing that Tiger Woods has done should reasonably inspire that much contempt.

title: 1/5  Lots of Marketing Fluff, Little Substance
text:
Want closeup photos of people exploding out of deep powder with fine snow crystals spraying everywhere, pics of cute ski bunnies, and photos of desserts or appetizers? How about a periodical that focuses on trendy terms like "vert," "avy" and "brah?" If you said yes, SKI is your magazine. Want photos showing the entire mountain or its views, as well as articles containing facts, statistics and useful information about ski resorts and equipment? Well, keep looking, SKI Magazine is too cool and sophisticated to bother with such pedestrian fare.

I would think that at least 50% of the reason most people would subscribe to SKI Magazine would be to obtain information on ski resorts for planning a skiing vacation. SKI Magazine is remarkably useless at providing the sort of information a real person, as opposed to some urban hipster marketing industry person who has never been on a mountain, would want to read about. In the magazine's annual best ski resort issue (the first issue of the season, mailed out in September), which ranks the top 50 resorts, most of the photos show a closeup of the aforementioned skier exploding out of powder or show some other closeup of a skier on snow, with no reference at all to the location. Is he in Colorado, Utah, British Columbia, Austria, Vermont...? Maybe even in the UP of Michigan? We can't tell - there's no background usually shown. Do most people base their vacations on where one can most likely find cute chiquitas with huge smiles wearing ski outfits? Apparently the folks at SKI Magazine think so - they always include several such photos as the solitatry photo for a particular place in their resort issue. The September 2013 (for the 2013-14 season) resort guide features a photo of a slice of chocolate cheesecake for one resort. Gee, I was thinking that a photo of the mountain views might help steer me in the right direction on picking a ski vacation destination, but no, how silly of me - that slice of cake is much more relevant.

The typical skier would like to see all of the following stats for each resort:

-Base and summit elevations
-Vertical drop
-Number of trails and total size in acres
-Breakdown of difficulty of trails (# of beginner, intermediate, expert)
-Number and type of lifts
-Annual snowfall and percentage of trails covered by snowmaking
-Season (e.g. November 20th to April 15th, weather permitting)
-Lift ticket cost

Out of the 50 resorts they boast of on the front cover of their resort issue (actually only 40 in the 2012-13 best resorts issue - in SKI Magazine math 30 Western resorts + 10 Eastern resorts = 50 total resorts), they gave vertical drops on maybe five resorts and about the same with annual snowfall or size in acres. They give no stats at all for at least half of the resorts, instead focusing on on-slope or resort area dining or how remote or cold its location is. About the only helpful information that the resort guide typically provides is information on any expansion (added lifts, new trails, new lodge facilities, increased snowmaking, etc...) a resort has made since the last season or maybe a comment on how the resort ranks for families or off-slope activities. In other issues, longer articles on ski resorts generally omit half or more of the list of basic stats, instead focusing for half a page on some new restaurant at the resort and its brilliant Swiss chef or the environmentally-conscious ruminations of the resort's new manager, which would be material information for somewhat fewer than a dozen people in the entire world in deciding what resort to ski for their next vacation.

I'm not sure how reliable their rankings are for resorts, anyway, since they are allegedly based on surveys from "over 10,000 SKI subscribers." For example, the allegedly #5 ranked ski resort in the East is Holiday Valley in New York. Could people genuinely have felt this 750' hill is a better resort than Stowe, Killington, Sugarbush and Whiteface, all of which rank below it? I've skied Holiday Valley and it never would have occurred to me that it would even be in the top 20 in the rankings of Eastern ski resorts, let alone the top-5. Perhaps the resort hired a firm to stuff the balot box, as marketing companies do for book and other product reviews on this and other websites.

Equipment reviews tend to contain so many generalized terms that they don't really help. They don't quantify anything, either based on actual figures that could quantify performance objectively, or on say, a more subjective 1-10 scale for the testers to use to rate particular characteristics. The magazine takes care not to ever say anything negative about any ski for fear of displeasing an advertiser. The only conclusion one can draw from reading SKI Magazine reviews of skis is that they are all good, since they don't provide any information to the contrary. On the topic of candor and negativity, they did say that Killington has been mismanaged in recent years but did not describe how or why - that is the only negative comment I can recall appearing about any advertiser in the past two years.

As for positives, well, the skiing techniques and tips tend to be pretty good, though - more clearly written and easier to understand than, say, the golf instruction articles in Golf or Golf Digest magazine. The beginning of each issue usually does contain some pretty amazing photos of mountains and skiers (although often only accessible by helicopter) that get one wishing for the first big snowfall. And finally, one can obtain subscriptions (6 issues/yr) pretty cheap from a variety of sources - I think I got a 3-year subscription from a magazine discounter for something like $12.

Overall, the negatives outweigh the positives with this magazine. The perspective tends to be about 50% Madison Avenue uber-cool junior advertising executive ("the on-slope bistro's saffron creme brulee is TO DIE FOR!"), 45% jaded semi-pro ski bum looking for fresh, back country double black diamond runs (Brah! Get out of your yurt and let's go munch some fresh pow!"), and about 5% regular, typical skier.

EDIT 9/14: Well, the September 2014 issue came out and its equipment guide now does use a numerical rating system for skis and boots, including both an overall rating and a value rating, although the latter appears to be somewhat arbitrary. There is a disclaimer at the end of the article, though, stating that all of the skis were good, so no advertiser's feelings get hurt. However, we have a continuation of the hipster language with a reference to "groms" in an article on teaching kids to ski (is a "grom" supposed to be hipster for "kid?"). And we have more arrogant assumptions without explanations - in a guide to back country skiing, there's a section on avalanche airbags, without ever mentioning what exactly they do (I looked one up on REI's website and they act much like flotation devices in water, keeping a skier on the top of the avalanche instead of being buried). An article on the Steamboat resort remains annoyingly free of useful statistics, as usual. Plus it seemed like more than half of the magazine was taken up by special advertising sections extending many pages for several ski resorts, meaning one has to wade through a whole lot of pages just to get to the magazine itself. So while the new equipment rating system is a step in the right direction, the rest of the magazine continues to emphasize attitude and advertisers at the expense of providing useful, informative information.

EDIT 3/2/16: I just reduced the rating for this magazine to 1/5 star. I did this for three reasons:

1) For subscription year 2015-16, they sent me a grand total of 3 issues. Either they omitted a bunch or have scaled back so thoroughly that they have literally halved the number of issues and thus halved the value of the product. I think it's therefore fair to halve my rating.

2) Although they are getting better than they were in 2014-15 and prior years, the magazine still features a significant number of model-skiers wearing hats, not helmets. This is reprehensible. Last year I rode a lift with a guy who pointed to the spot on the slope where a beginner had crashed into his best friend a dozen years ago, the spot where there was an icy patch, and the specific tree that his best friend had slid into head-first, splitting open his skull and killing him. He applauded my good sense in wearing a helmet and said that if his friend had been wearing one, he'd be alive and on the lift next to him that day instead feeding worms in some cemetery. This year I was on a lift that stopped for about a minute, 50 feet over a beginner (one could tell by her short rental skis) who didn't think she needed a helmet. I looked down, saw all the blood where her head hit a tree, and saw the Ski Patroller desperately trying to administer CPR to keep her alive, and realized he was probably just trying to keep her organs functioning enough to harvest them for organ donation - she was clearly dead. Yes, this is very sobering. It was rather traumatic for my elementary school-aged kid to see, also. The problem is that the general public thinks snow is soft (unlike asphalt for a helmet-free motorcyclist, the risk involved in skiing are not self-evident), no one at all at the ski resorts is adequately promoting helmets or describing the dangers and risks of this great sport, and then we keep seeing all these fabulous, glamorous, and insanely adventurous skiers in magazines who eschew a helmet for a trendy, colorful hat. Ski Magazine should be ashamed of itself for not making it mandatory to be wearing a helmet if a model wants to appear in the magazine. Neither my daughter nor I will ever forget the dead young woman we saw this year. I doubt many, if any, people at this magazine have any appreciation whatsoever for what is actually involved in skier safety and they are so badly dropping the ball by failing to promote helmets.

3) In all of the issues I've ever read over the years, Ski Magazine has never once addressed the issue of skier safety. That's right, they have never once published an article (at least not in the past 3 years or any other years I've subscribed) that addresses any aspect whatsoever about skier safety. Let's be blunt, the entire ski industry has lawyered-up and legislator-ed up like virtually no other industry, and as a consequence, no players in this market are doing anything other than the very bare minimum needed to avoid liability (for resorts, that means minimal compliance with the recreational immunity statute that protects them from suit by injured skiers, in the form of tiny, never-read warning print on their waiver forms). The only entity that I've seen in the ski industry that actually has taken any affirmative steps to promote skier safety is Breckenridge, which has very prominent signs up on a number of their lifts that serve intermediate, advanced and expert terrain "NO BEGINNERS." Ski magazine could serve as a valuable forum for promoting safety. Instead of some horse manure article on which resorts now have restaurants serving Pho (Vietnamese noodle soup), promote instead resorts that are going out of their way to keep people from getting injured. If there was a resort that adopted a mandatory helmets policy (see #2 above), promote and praise that resort and soon others would follow. Ski Magazine could take a leadership role in the ski industry in promoting safety and saving lives, but it does absolutely nothing, preferring to be driven by marketing concerns, not the concerns of genuine skiers.

EDIT 12/22/16: The January 2017 issue just arrived and it is crammed with articles and features that suggest to me that the magazine is run by people who neither know much about skiing nor care about the sport. I'll preface these critical comments by listing the positive first and stating that this issues article on Snowbird did list some important stats and did focus on a lot of relevant information about upgrades the resort has done or will complete in the next few years, so this was a marked improvement over most resort articles of the past few years. However, the issue also contained an article (one of several of a continuing series on automobiles) on full-sized SUVs that get better gas mileage. I don't know about you, but a ski magazine is just about the last place I'd consider as a source for what new vehicle to purchase. I'm pretty sure not a single person has ever sworn at how old, worn-out, in need of repair, etc... his or her car has become and then, behind the wheel or staring at it in the middle of the garage, suddenly said "Wait a second! I know where I'll turn for advice on my new ride - Ski Magazine!!"

The magazine's content continues to suggest that someone high on its editorial board came over from a culinary or wine magazine with no experience at all with skiing - they insist on trying to shoe-horn articles or prominent portions of articles about resorts on the topic of food and drink, in lieu of more relevant information about the actual skiing experience at those resorts. At least in the January 2017 article, it appears the author actually attended the particular food and wine event at Beaver Creek about which she was writing. Most of these articles that fill up pages of every issue do not seem to reflect that anyone from the magazine personally sampled the food mentioned in the articles, but could have been based on responses and photos supplied by resorts' marketing directors to inquiries about promoting the resorts' food and beverage options. People do take gastro-vacations, but their destinations are places like New Orleans, New York, San Francisco and the wine country, Chicago, etc.... Maybe a few dozen families each year take a resorts' restaurants into serious consideration when they plan a ski vacation.

That portion of the magazine that is created by genuine skiers continues to dedicate its focus to expert skiers. The cover story for this month's issue is skiing Alaska and almost all of the article is on heli-skiing, of interest really just to experts. Ski also used a ski-hipster term in that article that was new to me, derogatorily referring to "Herbs," I suppose to indicate non-experts or, people like me who do not know what a "Herb" is. The page on the Bear Mountain section of Killington is devoted to mogul runs. This focus is akin to car magazines devoting 70% of their reviews to 600hp supercars that 99% of their readership cannot afford.

Here's what I'd like to see included in this magazine, beyond what I've outlined above:

- At least one monthly article devoted to family ski trips - focus on what resorts have a good quantity of beginner and intermediate terrain, which have good kids skiing programs and instruction, which resorts have abundant nearby off-trail activities for that one family member who isn't as avid of a skier.

- A monthly instructional article aimed at transitioning skiers from the "can somewhat comfortably ski blues" to the competently handle black diamond terrain level of skill. The substantial majority of skiers fit someplace in or near this range of ability.

- Focus on skier safety. Every issue should have at least a half page devoted to skier safety and warning of the dangers of the sport.

- Every article on a resort should contain at least one panoramic photo of the main portion of the resort and a trail map with full mountain stats.

- More articles on skier fitness, particularly in the earlier issues. I skied probably 20 days at my local Midwestern ski area last year before a trip to Colorado and thought I was in pretty good ski shape, but was rather shocked at how my thighs felt like they were on fire going down 2000+ vertical feet of trails. I definitely would have done some exercises beforehand if I had a bit better warning of what to expect and some sort of instructional articles to read.

- A monthly article dedicated to the budget-minded skier or ski family. Have multiple tips about how to enjoy this great-but-expensive sport more economically. Not some hipster/internet hero/semi-comedic tale of crashing in the back of a VW van or in some ski hippy's teepee while dumpster-diving for dinner, but advice on resorts that give the best bang-for-the-buck, how and when to get discounted lift tickets or airfares, how to save on equipment and gear, etc.... I'll start by giving an example: on your next trip to Colorado, consider Loveland instead of the better known resorts. You get at least 100% of the views, scenery, and challenging terrain of the more prestigious resorts, at least 80% less crowds, their lift tickets can be frequently had discounted for about 1/3 of the cost of a Breckenridge or Vail lift ticket, and if one buys a Loveland season pass, it costs about what 3 days at Vail or Beaver Creek would cost and includes 3 days of skiing at Crested Butte, too.

title: An empty shell of a previously great magazine.
text:
Forbes used to be a great magazine. I had a subscription last year, and has it changed!

First, the majority of the magazine is advertisements. Fine, but you need to make up for it with good content.

The editorial/opinion pieces are great, however these are about two pages in the magazine. Mr Forbes always has something insightful. These are the reasons I am giving two stars. The magazine has a slight conservative approach to public financial policy, and I appreciate that, personally. If you lean more liberal, you probably won't even like these sections of the magazine.

Otherwise, the magazine has no other value; the financial advice is down right harmful in some cases. It is very pro active management when it comes to investing which time and time again has shown to be inferior to passive index investing.

The magazine also supports stock picking at times, which again, is proven to be bad advice for almost everyone regardless of wealth. This is shown in most modern investment studies

The cover stories are hardly interesting. This part is just my opinion, but I have no interest in reading about billionaires or other people's money. I want good insight. I feel like I'm reading a hollow entertainment magazine at times, except it dresses it up for supposedly "business people".

The magazine is in fact so poor, they are trying to get me to renew for a full year and a half for only $14 plus throwing in a watch for free. I might renew just for the watch.

All in all, save your money. I wish I could recommend a good financial/business magazine with similar policy leanings, but I cannot. If I find it, I'll report back.

Gosh I never knew cooking could be so... boring! Like many other reviewers, I was annoyed by the profuse amount of advertising included with a subscription to this magazing. The worst part is how each magazine has a dense construction paper-like front cover ad actually stapled into the binding of the magazine itself, which makes removing a hassle. So much for paying extra for a magazine without advertisements!

I generally subscribe to cooking magazines for inspiration to try new dishes, but the dull writing style and lack of pictures (especially color photos) in Cooks Illustrated really never made me very enthusiastic about the recipes. On the bright side, their more scientific approach to finding the 'optimum' recipe for a certain dish, and discovering the purpose of how adding ingredients led to a successful recipe, is quite interesting to a serious cook. I can certainly understand why some people enjoy this magazine, but it was not for me.

Considering a subsription to CI costs about twice as much as the other cooking magazines for only half of the issues, I felt that the magazine really lacked content or many interesting recipes.

Lastly, I originally subscribed to CI based on all of the positive reviews here on amazon, but to my disappointment I received three letters informing me that my subscription was running out and that I should resubscribe BEFORE I even received m first issue! title: Nice quality mag, but boring, colorless, "restful" interior decor
text:
I have subscribed to both The English Garden and The English Home in the past, but I decided a couple of years ago to drop The English Home, not because the quality of the magazine itself was lacking in any way -- the glossy, heavy pages are beautiful and there are hardly any ads, except a few very British ones that actually add to the English feel of the publication. No, it's because the house interiors shown are 90% boring, with bland, nearly colorless decor. Almost every room is painted white, cream, very light gray or some variation thereof, with pale furniture, carpets, curtains and perhaps a few pops of color in the accessories ventured by only the boldest of homeowners.

I know it is not TEH's fault that the English are going through a collective decorating phase in which they are pathologically afraid of bright or bold colors -- I theorize that this must have something to do with the social anxieties built into the British class system, with most middle-class people terrified of being "tasteless," or vulgar/common, the worst epithets one can hurl at an English person. Occasionally the magazine features rooms with beautifully colorful wallpapers covered with the over-sized flowers or birds that characterize the updated wallpaper styles after the bitty patterns of the 1980s. But I think most people are still recovering from the excesses of pattern that characterized the Laura Ashley era, and they therefore paint everything in "restful" pale tones. It's akin to the gardening phase when pastel flower colors were the only permissible colors and "hot" flower colors such as yellow, orange and red caused English people to feel faint and fan themselves on garden tours. The trend for American prairie plants has thankfully paved the way for more color in English gardens now, but the same cannot be said for English interiors. I crave beautiful colors!

Bottom line: if you adore pale interiors, you will love this magazine. If you like color, you may be just as disappointed as I was. The exteriors of English Homes are still lovely, with old cottages surrounded by cottage gardens, or beautiful stone manor houses set amid yew hedges and grand gardens. But the interiors are quite a disappointment, and I can't wait until the next era of English decorating asserts itself -- I hope color will be socially permitted.

title: Look to the Skies through your Telescope
text:
I recently purchased the March 2008 issue of "Sky & Telescope: The Essential Magazine of Astronomy." As expected, this magazine is filled with advertisements for various telescopes and components. With my interest in photography, I found most of the ads very interesting and spent more time viewing and reading the ads than I would have previously thought. My oldest son has a student telescope that we cannot seem to get to work properly. After he viewed the advertisements in this magazine he has asked for a telescope "upgrade."

In the middle of the magazine are various pull-out March 2008 star charts. I will admit that my first experience with the star chart was a bit intimidating and took several minutes to decipher. However, I have successfully used this chart to locate Ursa Major, Polaris, and Cassiopeia. Once our Upstate, NY skies clear again, I am looking forward to using this cart to help locate the Winter Circle and the accompanying constellations and stars.

This magazine features several articles each month. The featured articles of March 2008 include: "Cosmic Superparticle Mystery: Solved?" "Origin of the Elements of Life" "Where Did You Come From?" "Gaia's Mission to the Milky Way" and "Polestars of the Future: A Journey in a Celestial Time Machine." The second and third featured articles both interested me in this issue and both were also featured on the Cover of the magazine.

Within this magazine there are many "departments" that would appear every month including a monthly information regarding the sky in general (moon phases, planets that may be visible, and a celestial almanac), The Northern Hemisphere's Sky chart, A Binocular Highlight (tips and what can be seen using binoculars), The Southern Hemisphere's Sky chart, Sun Moon and Planets (what can be seen and expected by the various planets and our sun this month), Exploring the Moon (this month's article highlights craters and lunar impacts), Celestial Calendar (the path of asteroid 7 Iris is highlighted this month), Deep-Sky Wonders (highlighting the stars of Gemini), S&T Test Report (various telescopes, lenses, and parts are evaluated with specifications given), Spectrum (a short note written by the Editor), Letters by readers, Skyscape (Images of the sky), News Notes (short blurbs about recent discoveries and notable news), Mission Update (concerning space telescopes and observations), 50 & 25 Years Ago (discoveries from the past), New Product Showcase (highlights new products, lenses and telescopes that have just been released for consumers), Rambling Through the Skies (an article giving the history and mythology of constellations), Star Trails (general articles about stars, our Sun, Moon and comets), Books & Beyond (recommendations for various astronomy and telescope books), Astronomy Online (reviews of various on-line reference and astronomy related websites), Telescope Workshop (building your own telescope), Hobby Q&A (questions and answers related to amateur astronomy), Gallery (reader's images showcased), and Focal Point (a short, humorous article that closes that magazine).

Overall, I am highly impressed by the quality images and articles found in this magazine. There is such a range of information that any person looking at the night sky would be able to find an interesting article among this issue. The graphics and images that are included in this issue complement the articles and discussions that are presented. This is a highly informative magazine concerning technology and the night sky and I am already looking forward to the April 2008 issue next month.

title: Consumer Beware:  Consumer Reports Magazine "Auto Annual Renew" Option is not Optional
text:
A couple of days ago, I got online and subscribed to Consumer Reports Magazine. When the order was complete, the confirmation screen that popped up said that I had the "Auto Annual Renewal" option. Well, I hadn't seen any such option during the subscription process! So I went back to the subscription screen, and, sure enough, in tiny text, were the words:
"Safe Renew Offer: As an added benefit you will receive uninterrupted service and delivery of Consumer Reports, and your subscription will be automatically renewed at the lowest publicly available rate on our website. You won't be bothered with any renewal notices in the mail; instead, you will receive a clearly marked reminder at least 45 days before your credit card is charged. You may opt out of the automatic renewal program at anytime (sic) by contacting customer service."
Man, did I feel SAFE!!!!
I had to phone the Customer Service office twice (the first time I was told that my subscription hadn't yet hit their system, and to call back in 24 hours). The next time, a few minutes ago, I was told that "Auto Renew" was the only option for online subscriptions, but that I could opt out of the option by calling them up.
Now, that's not what I expect from a consumer-advocacy organization. Not even close.

In fairness, I did find out later that I could have downloaded this on my own and filled it out for free, but when notified by my tax preparer that I owed PA sales tax while I was standing there in his office, I did not know what other options there were. Overall, the best options are either for the publisher to find a way to collect the sales tax through Amazon if they are going to sell here, or the purchaser should be aware that the publisher will send a record of the sale to the state revenue department.

title: Favorite Cooking Magazine
text:
My Grandma gave me a few old copies of Cook's Country and now I'm hooked. I now own the complete collection of Cook's Country through both books and magazines. Having just thumbed through them all to create a recipe index, here's what I think:

Pros: No advertising. Recipes that actually work, the first time. Hardly any convenience products (i.e. mixes or cream of chicken soup) as ingredients. I'm a meat & potatoes kind of person, so I like the type of recipes they include. I also like that there aren't too many casseroles. The dishes focus on meat or on vegetables, making them easy to tweak for picky kids or guests with special dietary needs.

Cons: Large size means I can't fit them with my other cookbooks. Some of the recipes are too elaborate/expensive to make regularly (or at least on a weeknight). Some of the recipes are modified slightly and included again in later years. I am at a higher elevation (3500 feet) and stovetop recipes take a lot longer than they say they should. The recipes almost all use flour and/or butter/dairy, making them hard to modify for gluten-free or dairy-free diets.

That said, this is my favorite cooking magazine and the only one I currently subscribe to.

title: Why buy the magazine when you can watch ads on T.V. for free?
text:
...because that's all this magazine is: an advertising vehicle aimed at kids who aren't old enough to discriminate between ads and actual content yet.

Don't be fooled by the venerable "National Geographic" name: this publications pays only the briefest lip service to educational content. When my son received it as a gift I was shocked to see that the ads were virtually indistiguishable from the articles. And in fact, the ads were often much more visually interesting.

The photos were excellent, I must admit. But the layout was jazzed up to the point of absurdity, as if designed to play to kids with minuscule attention spans. The science facts were sound, but again, the articles were cut absurdly short, more like squibs and factoids than actual articles, as if the editors believe that kids couldn't possibly focus on one topic long enough to actually read more than 250 words about it...or maybe because they didn't want to distract the kids from all that tantalizingly lucrative advertising stuffed onto every page.

As an editor and a parent, I am appalled by this magazine and would not recommend it to anyone. National Geographic should be ashamed of itself for pushing this kind of junk on young readers. Avoid this publication like the plague.

title: High marks!
text:
I subscribed to this magazine one year ago. Out of the four issues I've received this year, I've knitted at least one project idea from each issue, and three so far from the fall issue alone (!) and each has turned out beautifully.

I haven't read any other knitting magazines that appeal to me as consistently as this one. I've noticed that each issue has a careful balance of projects, appealing to both genders and to all levels of knitting expertise.

Each issue contains a few "gee-whiz!" type articles in the front with interesting, exotic and sometimes downright weird news about the knitting world (like, who knew that knitting could be considered performance art?).

There's usually an exotic "catch-the-eye" or cutting-edge fashion project, followed by other apparel projects that are always beautiful, visually appealing and frequently wearable, too! Although the magazine does occasionally include items that make me shake my head in disbelief, Interweave Knits generally seems to select projects that real humans can wear without looking like freaks.

You'll also find a couple of ideas for non-apparel and/or "quick gift"-type projects in each issue, ranging from felted backpacks and novelty purses to baby hats.

Now, if all this sounds good, just wait: it gets better. The real clincher for me is that the patterns seem to have been tested and carefully proof-read BEFORE going to press. I've worked 7 projects from IWK this year, and have yet to catch a single mistake in pattern directions! Maybe I've just been lucky so far, but I noticed on the IWK website that the list of errata is amazingly short...so either they don't update errata onto their website, or they really don't allow a lot of mistakes to slip through.

In short, I think "Interweave Knits" provides a lot of bang for your subscription bucks. Two thumbs up from me!

title: Martha isn't just for your mother!
text:
There is a reason that people place ads on Craigslist looking for old Martha Stewart magazines, and why they sell for a pretty penny on Ebay. Martha Stewart Living is a great magazine for those who really like to try their hand at creation of all sorts.Being a thirty-something gal who is learning to cook, bake, garden, can, decorate and entertain, I am in love with this magazine. Not only is it beautiful from cover to cover with stunning photography and eye-catching layouts, it is filled with ideas and inspiration for young women like myself who are coming into their adult lives who want to make a house feel like a home and who want to host signature events.

Having grown up fed processed foods and taking weekly family grocery trips to the Costco, I never knew the power of tending a garden or making jam. Now,I feel empowered when I create pizza dough from scratch, or make my home beautiful for a party, or create that special greeting card with help from this magazine. Martha Stewart Living is a reminder to all of us that we can do things for ourselves.

Some reviewers have said that ideas in the magazine are out-of-touch, or too costly due to specialized equipment, and that is true. Some of the ideas in this magazine are not five and dime craft time with baby projects - some are very sophisticated and I appreciate that, even if I cannot participate myself just yet. Most the ideas in this magazine are very accessible to anyone who can afford the subscription. SO much so that for Christmas I bought a gift subscription for my best friend who lives far away from me. Each month, we call each other the day our magazines arrive and get excited about the new ideas together.

My Martha Stewart Living magazines are craft/entertainment library treasures. I look at them time and time again and cannot imagine ever not wanting to keep each issue - now isn't that saying something about the quality of the product? I think so.
